attacks.name: GTIG finds an exposed exploit_agent server that diffs patches and runs exploits
attacks.researcher: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor

sources.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold

attacks.ai_role_detail: The exposed server hosted a multi-agent framework, exploit_agent, that uses frontier and local LLMs to diff patched web-application code, draft exploits, and run them without a human in the loop.
attacks.technique_summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant (Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, and David Mainor, 16 November 2026) say that in the past quarter GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop. One case was an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework named exploit_agent. It integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework continuously diffs popular web-application software, comparing code before and after patch announcements, analyzes the diff for vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and executes them without human intervention. On the server, with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, GTIG found scripts for internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers' webshells. Victim telemetry on the server indicated interest in French websites in media and entertainment, and in education. A published sample shows the framework inspecting access-control code in the Spectra (Ultimate Addons for Gutenberg) WordPress plugin, version 2.19.25. An environment-file comment, in Russian, labels LLM API keys for auto-exploitation and tells the operator to write the keys in that file rather than in chat. GTIG does not name the operator, a country, or a public repository for exploit_agent. The Russian comment is an artifact on the server, not a stated victim or actor country.
attacks.initial_access: Exposed staging server. For the victim sites, the report says the framework drafts and runs exploits against web applications. It does not name the vulnerability used at each site.
ai_tooling_and_models: Frontier and local LLMs, models not named
other_tooling: Scripts for reconnaissance, brute force, webshell install, and webshell removal
attacks.victims_and_sectors: French websites in media and entertainment, and in education. No organization is named.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. GTIG and Mandiant identified the exposed server. No cluster name and no country are stated.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: One exposed staging server. Victim telemetry indicated French media, entertainment, and education sites. No victim count was published.
attacks.prevention_angle: Treat a short patch window on internet-facing web applications as the defensive problem this report describes. Review Spectra (Ultimate Addons for Gutenberg) 2.19.25 and later plugin updates, unexpected PHP writes under plugin directories, webshell install and removal, reconnaissance and brute-force scripts on web servers, and outbound use of newly captured data. No public exploit_agent repository was identified.
attacks.source_notes: The server, the exploit_agent name, the no-human-in-the-loop diff-and-execute loop, the post-compromise scripts, the French sector targeting, the Spectra 2.19.25 sample, and the Russian environment-file comment are from the 16 November 2026 GTIG tracker. The Russian text is quoted there as an LLM API-key comment for the exploit_agent pilot. It is not used as a country. GTIG published no repository URL. Searches during this review did not find a public exploit_agent project to link. No IP addresses, domains, or file hashes were published for this server.
attacks.region_notes: France is the victim-website geography GTIG stated. The Russian-language environment comment is an artifact on the staging server, not a victim region and not an attributed actor country.

atlas_techniques.rationale: GTIG found a deployed multi-agent software framework, exploit_agent, built to research and weaponize web-application patches.

attacks.name: Suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE uses SynthID recruiter lures and Claude Code settings to deploy SOMBERMEME
attacks.researcher: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor

sources.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold

attacks.ai_role_detail: SynthID watermarks on fake recruiter photos and likely LLM-authored ClickFix scripts are adversary use of generative models. The same intrusions then change .claude/settings.json so the victim's Claude Code launch downloads SOMBERMEME.
attacks.technique_summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group (Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, and David Mainor, 16 November 2026) describes suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE activity in the DPRK section of the quarterly tracker. In recent intrusions against cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe, the cluster used LLM-enabled social engineering and the victim organization's AI tools as an internal supply-chain vector. For access, the actor created fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms. The profile images contained SynthID watermarks, which GTIG says confirms LLM-synthesized identities. The personas sent targets to fraudulent meeting platforms with ClickFix lures that asked them to run diagnostic fix scripts. GTIG calls those staging scripts likely LLM-authored. After the initial compromise, the actor changed .claude/settings.json in internal code repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor. The actor also created GitHub personal access tokens named after Microsoft Copilot. GTIG places this in a broader observation that DPRK operators use generative tools for scale and use native agent execution hooks for enterprise access. No IP addresses, hashes, domains, or public tool repository were published for this cluster.
attacks.initial_access: Fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms, then ClickFix lures on fraudulent meeting pages that ask the target to run a diagnostic fix script.
ai_tooling_and_models: LLM image generation, evidenced by SynthID watermarks
other_tooling: GitHub personal access tokens named after Microsoft Copilot
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe. No organization is named.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE. GTIG describes the activity under Democratic People's Republic of Korea threat actors. The cluster name and the country are both stated as suspected.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: GTIG says multiple intrusions over the course of 2026 used this combination, and describes recent intrusions against cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe. No victim count was published.
attacks.prevention_angle: Review professional-network recruiter approaches that lead to a meeting page and a pasted diagnostic script. Diff .claude/settings.json in internal repositories, and alert when a process rewrites a file under .claude/ before Claude Code starts a download. Review new GitHub personal access tokens, including tokens whose names refer to Microsoft Copilot. No SOMBERMEME hash or domain was published.
attacks.source_notes: The cluster name, SynthID watermarks, ClickFix meeting pages, the likely LLM-authored scripts, the .claude/settings.json change, SOMBERMEME, the Copilot-named GitHub tokens, and the North America and Europe cryptocurrency targeting are from the 16 November 2026 GTIG tracker. Category is adversary-use-of-ai because the operator used generative models for the recruiter imagery and, GTIG says, likely for the staging scripts. The change to the victim's Claude Code settings is ai_role_secondary ai_agent_or_mcp_as_target. That split matches other entries that contain both an operator role and abuse of an AI tool, and the category order in scripts/import-notion.mjs. No frameworks value is set. GTIG did not name an offensive framework for this cluster, and did not publish a command line or a host platform for the ClickFix script.
attacks.region_notes: North America and Europe are the target regions GTIG named. North Korea is the suspected actor country, not a victim region.

attacks.name: Symantec - AI-assisted commands revived a stalled intrusion at a US retailer

sources.title: How AI revived a stalled attack on a U.S. retailer
How AI revived a stalled attack on a U.S. retailer
How AI revived a stalled attack on a U.S. retailer
EfsPotato
Chisel
Yuze

attacks.ai_role_detail: Symantec rates AI assistance high confidence and an operator-in-the-loop, rather than an autonomous agent, at moderate confidence. The model was not identified. Gaps between scripts never fell below seven seconds.
attacks.technique_summary: Symantec Threat Hunter Team (Broadcom; SECURITY.COM article created Nov 16, 2026) describes a September 2026 intrusion at a U.S. retailer. The initial access vector is unknown. The earliest activity, Sep 18, was on three Microsoft SQL Server hosts, with cmd.exe running under sqlservr.exe, which Symantec treats as likely xp_cmdshell. Some of those commands were already long PowerShell scripts with quoted section labels. The scripts searched point-of-sale synchronization directories for stored passwords and connection strings, tested egress to 155.254.22[.]215:9458, and on one host appended base64 text under ProgramData, decoded it with Certutil, and compiled it with csc.exe. The source was EfsPotato (https://github.com/zcgonvh/EfsPotato). The payload saved the SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives. On Sep 21 an internet-facing IIS server appeared, with commands under w3wp.exe. On Sep 22 the commands looked hand-typed: 110 actions, three typos including systemifo and pwoershell, average length about 45 characters. Loaders were killed by security software, including a Bitdefender bdreinit.exe sideload of log.dll and log.txt from 204.194.49[.]129:8080, a pairing also seen with ShadowPad loaders and not unique to one actor. The operators reran that loader about five times in 20 minutes. They also staged an AES PowerShell reverse shell, server.ps1, toward 166.0.25[.]106:443 with a fallback host at 154.81.37[.]136, and wrote ASP webshells filemanager.asp and qwdajhsd.asp. On Sep 23 they staged a G DATA ask.exe/ask.dll sideload and BreakChainC.exe, then switched to about 50 long, error-free PowerShell scripts over about two hours. Banners included ===FILES MENTIONING CONN STRINGS===. Comments stated a hypothesis, cited earlier results, and revised a conclusion, which Symantec reads as model reasoning pasted into a webshell. The scripts collected connection strings, the FileZilla Server user database, WinSCP, PuTTY, and RDP settings, IIS configuration, and Windows logon registry values. They found SolarWinds Orion, read its bundled RabbitMQ .erlang.cookie, and ran Orion's erl.exe so rpc:call reached os:cmd on a second server. The command was passed as decimal character codes. That was about 10 minutes after the first Orion query. Later the same day BreakChainCs.exe relaunched the sideloaded binaries through WMI and shell modes so they were no longer children of w3wp.exe. From Sep 24 to Sep 29 the activity reached more SQL servers, a host that looks like a domain controller, Chisel, a password sprayer, and searches for NTDS.dit, Group Policy Preferences passwords, and LAPS. No data theft or encryption was observed. Symantec's financial-motive reading rests on the point-of-sale password search, contact with 155.254.22[.]215 (named in a separate Sep 22 Gambit Security report as an AI console tied to card-skimming activity), and later domain-credential theft that could be ransomware preparation. Loader files and the staging server overlap an August intrusion elsewhere and a July intrusion at a securities firm; neither of those showed AI assistance. Yuze (https://github.com/P001water/yuze) was used in the August case back to 204.194.49[.]129. Trend Micro has documented Yuze use by Warlock operators (Symantec Longlegs, also known as Storm-2603). Symantec does not attribute this intrusion to them. ATT&CK techniques in the report include T1574.002, T1505.003, T1552.001, T1021, and T1003.002.
attacks.initial_access: Unknown. The first observed commands were cmd.exe under sqlservr.exe on SQL Server, consistent with xp_cmdshell, and later cmd.exe under w3wp.exe on IIS.
ai_tooling_and_models: Unidentified model. Symantec assesses AI-written PowerShell with an operator relaying output, not an autonomous agent.
other_tooling: EfsPotato (https://github.com/zcgonvh/EfsPotato), compiled on the server with csc.exe
Yuze (https://github.com/P001water/yuze), seen in the overlapping August intrusion
attacks.victims_and_sectors: A U.S. retail organization. Internet-facing IIS and at least six further servers, most of them Microsoft SQL Server. Point-of-sale synchronization scripts were searched for passwords.
attacks.region_notes: The primary victim is a U.S. retailer. The August and July overlaps are different organizations and are not given countries in the retailer write-up.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Symantec does not tie the activity to Warlock, Longlegs, or Storm-2603. ShadowPad-associated sideloading and Yuze are shared with other actors and are not treated as an attribution.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Sep 18 through at least Sep 29, 2026. On Sep 23, about 50 scripts in about two hours, median length over 500 characters, against about 45 characters for the earlier hand-typed commands. About 10 minutes from the first Orion query to command execution on a second server. No theft or encryption observed in this intrusion.
attacks.prevention_angle: Alert when w3wp.exe or sqlservr.exe spawns cmd.exe or PowerShell, and when xp_cmdshell is used. Treat a same-directory unsigned DLL next to bdreinit.exe or ask.exe as sideloading. Alert on csc.exe compiling from ProgramData or a user-writable path, on Chisel client arguments, and on reg save of SAM, SYSTEM, or SECURITY. Hunt Orion's bundled erl.exe making rpc:call with a cookie, and ASP files dropped in the web application's image directory. A sudden change from short mistyped commands to long labelled scripts is an investigation lead, not a benign automation signature. Restrict xp_cmdshell, the Erlang distribution port, and the RabbitMQ cookie file.
attacks.source_notes: Dates, typos, script counts, the Orion cookie path, the decimal-encoded rpc:call, and the published hashes are from the Symantec article at https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ai-assisted-attack-us-retailer (canonical; the blog-post URL serves the same title). The article's createdDate is 2026-11-16. Symantec lists many additional file hashes; the set below is the named tooling from that table, not every unnamed suspicious file. Yuze's Warlock reporting is Symantec's summary of Trend Micro, and Symantec says it is not an attribution. Link the August staging overlap only as Symantec describes it.

atlas_techniques.rationale: Symantec says the operators obtained working PowerShell, including the Orion cookie handoff, from an AI tool after hand-typed commands failed.
The AI-assisted phase was long PowerShell submitted through the webshell and through SQL Server command execution.
The scripts collected connection strings, client settings, the Erlang cookie, and registry hives that hold credential material.

nodes.description: About 10 minutes after the first Orion query, the operators read the RabbitMQ cookie and use the bundled erl.exe rpc:call path to run a command on a second server. Later activity dumps credential hives. No encryption was observed.

detections.name: Suspicious Process By Web Server Process
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for w3wp. Windows process creation. A web-server parent, including w3wp.exe, spawning a suspicious child. Matches commands Symantec saw under the IIS worker. It does not match sqlservr.exe as the parent.

detections.name: Suspicious Child Process Of SQL Server
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for sqlservr. Windows process creation. sqlservr.exe spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or another listed child. Matches the Sep 18 pattern Symantec reads as xp_cmdshell.

detections.name: MSSQL XPCmdshell Suspicious Execution
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for xp_cmdshell. Windows application log. MSSQL audit event 33205 whose data contains object_name:xp_cmdshell and statement:EXEC. Requires the xp_cmdshell audit policy. The process-creation rule above still applies when that audit policy is off.

detections.name: Windows Unsigned DLL Side-Loading In Same Process Path
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for DLL side-loading. Sysmon image load. An unsigned DLL loaded from the same directory as the process, outside Windows and Program Files. Fits bdreinit.exe with log.dll and ask.exe with ask.dll staged in the same folder. A signed decoy executable does not have to be on a named-binary list.

detections.name: Privilege Escalation via Rogue Named Pipe Impersonation
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for Potato. The rule cites https://github.com/zcgonvh/EfsPotato and alerts on Sysmon pipe-creation event 17 when the pipe path contains a nested Pipe segment. It does not match the string EfsPotato. The Splunk Potato-family rule's file-name list does not include EfsPotato, so that rule is not cited. A renamed compile can still miss a name-based hunt.

detections.name: Dynamic .NET Compilation Via Csc.EXE
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for csc.exe. Windows process creation. csc.exe whose command line points at ProgramData, Temp, or another listed user-writable location. Symantec compiled under ProgramData. The rule filters a w3wp.exe parent, so a compile whose parent is only the IIS worker does not match.

detections.name: PUA - Chisel Tunneling Tool Execution
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search for chisel. Windows process creation. Image ending in chisel.exe, or command lines with client/server and reverse, socks, or r: arguments. Symantec's Chisel detection on Sep 25 was on a Windows host. The Linux Chisel rule is not cited.

detections.name: Windows Registry Entries Exported Via Reg
detections.notes: Selected from a security-detections-mcp search under T1003.002. Endpoint process data. reg.exe with save or export. Symantec says the EfsPotato payload saved the SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives. This matches that copy when it is reg.exe. A custom writer that does not call reg.exe will not match.

detections.name: Erlang rpc:call and the Orion cookie
detections.notes: security-detections-mcp search for erl.exe returned no rule. Nothing in the index alerts on Orion's bundled erl.exe, rpc:call, or a read of .erlang.cookie. Hunt process creation for erl.exe under the Orion Erlang path with -setcookie and rpc:call. ASP names filemanager.asp and qwdajhsd.asp, and BreakChainC.exe, are also absent from the index; the w3wp child-process rule covers shells spawned from the web worker, not the ASP file drop by itself.

updates.summary: First activity on three SQL Server hosts. Labelled PowerShell searches point-of-sale sync folders, tests egress to 155.254.22[.]215:9458, and compiles EfsPotato on one host.
Commands start under w3wp.exe on the internet-facing web server, then pause for about 12 hours.
Hand-typed commands with typos. bdreinit.exe/log.dll from 204.194.49[.]129:8080 is killed on each retry. server.ps1 and two ASP webshells are staged.
About 50 long scripts in about two hours. Orion's Erlang cookie is used to run a command on a second server roughly 10 minutes after the first Orion query. BreakChainCs.exe follows.
Further SQL hosts save registry hives. Activity continues through at least Sep 29, including Chisel, NTDS.dit searches, and a password sprayer.
SECURITY.COM publishes the retailer write-up. AI assistance is high confidence; the operator-in-the-loop reading is moderate; the model is unidentified.

attacks.name: Dynatrace mcpvenom measures MCP tool-description poisoning across 12 frameworks

sources.title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
mcpvenom

attacks.borderline_note: This is a lab measurement with planted secrets and a canary server. The paper does not describe an intrusion against a named organization. All five vendor disclosures were rejected.
attacks.ai_role_detail: A malicious MCP server sits beside a legitimate one. Its tool descriptions, schema text, or tool responses are copied into the model prompt. The measured harm is the legitimate http_post tool sending a planted secret to a canary.
attacks.technique_summary: Farooq Shaikh and Biagio Montaruli (Dynatrace; AISec at ACM CCS 2026, Nov 15-19, The Hague) measure MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. mcpvenom (https://github.com/dynatrace-research/mcpvenom) runs 45 scenarios across 12 frameworks and 18 models, 9,720 cells. The attacker controls one MCP server the user installed and can change tool descriptions, input-schema descriptions, and tool responses. The attacker cannot change the system prompt, user messages, framework code, or model weights. A legitimate server exposes read_file, write_file, list_files, http_get, and http_post. A planted secret sits in the workspace. A canary HTTP server on port 18080 records exfiltration. Overall, 2,113 cells were vulnerable (22.9 percent). Of those, 64.9 percent were a dispatched attacker tool call, 23.0 percent were confirmed network contact, and 12.1 percent were a verified secret in the canary log. Hand review covered 1,259 transcripts. Nine core frameworks clustered between 23 and 26 percent, and the paper says none of the 12 implements an intentional description check. Pydantic AI's duplicate-tool-name rejection landed at 16.6 percent, and AG2's executor constraints at 4.6 percent. A regex scanner the authors built rejected 20 of 45 scenarios and flagged 9 of 125 benign descriptions (7.2 percent). Model results ran from Claude Fable 5 at 0.4 percent to Amazon Nova Pro at 49.7 percent (245 of 493 cells). Claude Opus 4.8 was vulnerable in 8 of 530 cells (1.5 percent) and issued 223 refusals that cited the poisoned description. Claude Sonnet 5 sometimes named the text as prompt injection and then made the exfiltration call. The simplest high-signal payload appends an instruction to read /workspace/.env and send it with http_post. That direct-description class scored 29.2 percent aggregate ASR outside AG2. A language-switch payload scored 66.0 percent. Five disclosures to four organizations were rejected: two to LangChain, one to Microsoft for AutoGen via MSRC, one to the MCP SDK, and one to Haystack (deepset). The AutoGen rejection is about microsoft/autogen, which the paper says is not the AG2 0.14.0 fork in the matrix. Link invariant-mcp-tool-poisoning-2025-04, the earlier description-poisoning report this paper cites.
attacks.initial_access: The user installs an MCP server whose tool description, schema text, or tool response carries the instruction. The paper's servers run over stdio in the lab.
ai_tooling_and_models: 12 MCP frameworks, including LangChain 1.5.0, Pydantic AI 2.14.1, CrewAI 1.15.5, Semantic Kernel 1.44.0, Haystack 3.0.0, and AG2 0.14.0
18 models, from Claude Fable 5 (0.4 percent) to Amazon Nova Pro (49.7 percent)
other_tooling: Legitimate http_post tool used to send the planted secret
attacks.victims_and_sectors: No customer is named. The matrix uses planted workspace secrets and framework harnesses.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: No threat actor. Dynatrace Research ran the measurement. The five vendor reports were rejected.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: 9,720 cells. 2,113 vulnerable (22.9 percent), including 255 cells (12.1 percent of the vulnerable set) with a canary receipt of the secret. 45 scenarios. 12 frameworks. 18 models.
attacks.prevention_angle: Review an MCP server's tool descriptions before adding it, and treat a description that names another tool, a file such as .env, or an outbound URL as hostile. Do not assume the framework checks that text. The paper's own regex scanner missed 25 of 45 scenarios, so a description scan is only a partial control. Prefer a model that refused in this matrix, and still review the server, because the paper says no framework defense made up for a susceptible model.
attacks.source_notes: Counts, model rates, framework versions, the http_post payload, the canary port, and the five rejections are from the paper text at https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03555. The workshop dates are Nov 15-19, 2026. The paper does not give a separate preprint day, so date_reported is the workshop start. Link invariant-mcp-tool-poisoning-2025-04.
attacks.region_notes: The Hague is the workshop location, not a victim region. Downloads in the paper's framework table are as of May 2026 and are not a victim count.

atlas_techniques.rationale: Tool descriptions, schema text, and tool responses are attacker-controlled fields copied into the model prompt
The successful cells invoke a legitimate tool, most clearly http_post, because the poisoned description told the model to
The verified tier is a planted workspace secret received by the canary HTTP server

nodes.title: Malicious MCP server is installed
nodes.description: The user adds a server the attacker published. It is registered next to a legitimate server that can read files and call http_post.

nodes.title: Poisoned description enters the prompt
nodes.description: Frameworks copy tool descriptions, schema text, and tool responses into the model context. The paper says none of the 12 checks that text on purpose.

nodes.title: http_post carries the secret

nodes.title: Canary confirms exfiltration

attacks.name: Amazon MadPot records ARTEX agents hunting AI provider keys and attempting exchange KYC deepfakes

sources.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents
Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys

attacks.ai_role_detail: MadPot decoys that presented LLM chat-completion APIs received ARTEX agents' own campaign memory, including prompts, tool history, and the shared knowledge graph.
attacks.technique_summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence (CJ Moses, AWS Security Blog, 13 November 2026) says that from 3 October to 5 November 2026, MadPot decoys configured as popular LLM chat-completion APIs received requests from AI agents. The requests carried persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and reported findings. Amazon assesses with moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, from prompt references to ARTEX tooling and other ARTEX artifacts, and with moderate confidence that the operators were disparate Chinese-nexus groups, from simplified Chinese prompts, China time-zone settings, targeting consistent with Chinese interests, and tooling predominantly used by Chinese-nexus threats. Standing instructions set mission, targeting, and constraints, including a fixed country sequence, a preference for enterprise production sites over personal projects, a ban on mainland China targets and government domains, and a requirement that outbound traffic use proxies. Credentials exposed for more than 30 days were to be treated as low-value. Most activity split work across planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a knowledge graph. Campaign 1, in the agents' records, hunted internet-exposed AI gateways and application builders, extracted upstream provider keys, validated them, and pooled them. Named targets were One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, LiteLLM, Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. The recorded playbook mapped each product to known chains, including uninitialized installs, anonymous management and provider-configuration endpoints, the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow), CVE-2026-28797 (RAGFlow), an isCliRequest authentication bypass on One API family systems, SSRF through URL-fetch features to cloud metadata services, and secrets in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files. Discovery used internet scanning, certificate transparency, GitHub repositories and event archives, npm and PyPI tarballs, container layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram. Stolen keys were fed into the framework gateway so stolen inference funded more hunting. Cloud credentials were validated, storage was enumerated, and managed AI services, secrets stores, and application identities were prioritized over general cloud permissions. Leads were graded L1, L2 for a working API call, and L3 for quantified impact. Campaign 2, in concurrent sessions against two cryptocurrency exchanges, attempted real-time deepfake video for liveness checks and forged ID-document photos. The agents' records say the vendor's server-side verdict rejected the deepfake on every recorded attempt. Amazon did not say whether the forged document photos passed. At least four sessions ran at once, on cash-out, balances, the deepfake pipeline, and the verification bypass. Amazon did not observe the described activity on other organizations as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported. It notified potentially affected AWS customers. Community forks that answered HTTP 200 on 16 November 2026 are https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX and https://github.com/MoLeft/ARTEX. The original Autumn-27/ARTEX repository returned HTTP 404.
attacks.initial_access: The agents' records describe exposed AI management interfaces, default credentials, known product flaws, and public artifact searches. Amazon did not observe those intrusions on customer or third-party systems.
ai_tooling_and_models: LLM chat-completion APIs, as presented by MadPot
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Agents' records describe hundreds of targets across AI application platforms and other workloads, plus two cryptocurrency exchanges. Amazon notified potentially affected AWS customers. No organization is named here.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed Chinese-nexus groups. Amazon Threat Intelligence, moderate confidence, from simplified Chinese prompts, China time zones, targeting, and tooling. Financially motivated. Not a single named cluster.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: MadPot collection window 3 October through 5 November 2026. The records describe hundreds of targets. Campaign 2 names two cryptocurrency exchanges and at least four concurrent agent sessions. Every recorded liveness verdict rejected the deepfake. No confirmed victim count was published.
attacks.prevention_angle: Put AI gateways, application builders, and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems. Change default credentials, including the LiteLLM default master key, and do not leave an install uninitialized. Remove unauthenticated management and provider-configuration endpoints. Review Langflow for CVE-2025-3248 and RAGFlow for CVE-2026-28797, and do not trust an isCliRequest header as authentication on One API family systems. Alert on URL-fetch features that can reach cloud metadata, and on secrets in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files. Watch provider spend. Treat the published IPs as MadPot observations of agent traffic in the stated windows, and corroborate them before blocking.
attacks.source_notes: The campaigns, the moderate-confidence attribution, the product list, the CVEs, the isCliRequest bypass, the SSRF and secret locations, the knowledge-graph roles, the two exchanges, the rejected liveness checks, and the eleven IPs are from the Amazon blog. Amazon states that it did not watch the off-decoy activity and cannot verify agent-reported outcomes. The Hacker News article of 16 November 2026 restates that blog. It also discusses Cloudflare and other ARTEX reporting that is not part of this entry. The Hacker News flaw table says Langflow versions before 1.3.0 are affected by CVE-2025-3248; Amazon's blog names the CVE and does not give that version range. https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX and https://github.com/MoLeft/ARTEX returned HTTP 200 on 16 November 2026. https://github.com/Autumn-27/ARTEX returned HTTP 404 and is not linked. Mainland China appears only as an operator exclusion, not as a victim region.
attacks.region_notes: Amazon describes a fixed country sequence and an instruction to exclude mainland China and government domains. It does not name the countries of the hundreds of targets or of the two exchanges. Those instructions are not recorded as victim regions.

atlas_techniques.rationale: Amazon assesses the captured agents were running the ARTEX offensive framework.
The recorded playbook steals provider keys from exposed gateways, default credentials, client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files.
Stolen keys were validated with provider identity services and fed into the framework gateway as working credentials.
A second campaign recorded real-time deepfake video and forged ID photos aimed at cryptocurrency-exchange KYC checks. Recorded liveness verdicts rejected the deepfake.

There is no detection rule in the index for a rejected liveness deepfake.

attacks.name: Elastic CyberStrikeAI server reads AWS user data, secrets, and sends an SSM command
attacks.researcher: Samir Bousseaden, Bryan Porras Blanch, Terrance DeJesus

sources.title: 56 AWS API calls in 141 milliseconds: Inside an AI-run intrusion
CyberStrikeAI

attacks.ai_role_detail: Elastic attributes the AWS calls to a CyberStrikeAI server from scan data and machine-speed CloudTrail. Elastic says it cannot prove an LLM agent made the decisions and does not know how the credentials were stolen.
attacks.technique_summary: Elastic Security Labs (Samir Bousseaden, Bryan Porras Blanch, Terrance DeJesus; Nov 13, 2026) describes one CyberStrikeAI server, 43.240.29.11 (AS133199, SonderCloud Limited, Hong Kong), using stolen credentials for eight identities across four AWS accounts from Sep 30 to Oct 16, 2026. Five were IAM users and three were EC2 instance roles. The role sessions were named after instance IDs, and using them from an outside IP means the credentials were taken off the instances. Activity fell on four days and produced 78 alerts, all medium or low, which Elastic says only cohered once correlated by source IP. On Sep 30 the server called GetCallerIdentity on four IAM users across three accounts within 51 minutes, three of those calls in the same second, plus GetSessionToken. The same day app-role read Secrets Manager and then issued 56 DescribeInstanceAttribute userData calls in 141 milliseconds (about 2.5 ms per call), part of 57 user-data reads from one assumed-role session that day and 58 user-data alerts overall. On Oct 1 it revalidated credentials, read more secrets with app-role, and used nonprod-role for two GetSecretValue calls. On Oct 2 container-role called GetParameter with decryption on an SSM SecureString and SendCommand 29 seconds later. CloudTrail does not show the command text or whether it succeeded. After 14 quiet days, on Oct 16 the server called GetSessionToken for a previously unseen user in a fourth account and rechecked two earlier users. Internet scan data showed 43.240.29.11 serving a CyberStrikeAI page on port 8080, with a self-signed certificate (CN CyberStrikeAI, serial 3356730520974368630, issued 2026-09-15), one day before the first alert. 43.240.29.28 and 43.240.29.33 served the same page, FOFA fid, and certificate but were not in this AWS telemetry. Elastic says none of the three was still serving that interface as of November 2026. Six Elastic rules fired: AWS EC2 User Data Retrieval for EC2 Instance (58, medium), AWS STS GetCallerIdentity API Called for the First Time (11, medium), First Time Seen AWS Secret Value Accessed in Secrets Manager (4, medium), AWS STS GetSessionToken Usage (3, low), AWS SSM SendCommand Execution by Rare User (1, low), and AWS Systems Manager SecureString Parameter Request with Decryption Flag (1, medium). Elastic added two high-severity rules: AWS EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration (more than 20 distinct instances in 10 minutes) and AWS STS GetCallerIdentity Bulk Account Enumeration (three or more distinct non-role identities from the same external IP and ASN in 10 minutes). Elastic, citing Will Thomas at Team Cymru, says 21 CyberStrikeAI IPs were counted in early 2026, aimed at Fortinet edge devices, and that this is the first Elastic case of the same tooling turned on AWS. The repository contains 24 SKILL.md files, including skills/unlimited-attack-scope/SKILL.md and skills/cloud-attack-methods/SKILL.md. Elastic cites https://github.com/Ed1s0nZ/CyberStrikeAI, which redirects to https://github.com/AIPentest/CyberStrikeAI. Link kaspersky-cyberstrikeai-schools-2026 and trendai-chinese-language-operators-used-cyberstrikeais-2026-10.
attacks.initial_access: Stolen AWS credentials for five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles, used from an external IP. Elastic does not know how the credentials were obtained.
ai_tooling_and_models: 24 SKILL.md files in the repository, including unlimited-attack-scope and cloud-attack-methods
other_tooling: AWS APIs GetCallerIdentity, GetSessionToken, GetSecretValue, DescribeInstanceAttribute, GetParameter, SendCommand
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Four AWS accounts. Account and identity names were replaced with aliases. No sector was named.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed operator. Elastic confirms the source IP served CyberStrikeAI. No country or motivation is stated. Hong Kong is the hosting location.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: One server, eight identities, four accounts, 78 alerts, four active days from Sep 30 to Oct 16, 2026. Fifty-six userData calls in 141 milliseconds. Sixty-five of 78 alerts fell on Sep 30.
attacks.prevention_angle: Rotate every identity that touched 43.240.29.11 and revoke active sessions. Replace instance profiles whose role credentials were used off-instance. Treat secrets in EC2 user data as exposed. Review SSM command history for the Oct 2 SendCommand. Restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData. Correlate medium and low CloudTrail alerts by source IP across multi-day gaps.
attacks.source_notes: API sequence, alert counts, rule names, certificate serial 3356730520974368630, and the three IPs are from the Elastic article. Only 43.240.29.11 appeared in the AWS alerts. The 24 SKILL.md count was checked on the repository default branch on 2026-11-15. Elastic cites https://github.com/Ed1s0nZ/CyberStrikeAI; that URL redirected to https://github.com/AIPentest/CyberStrikeAI. Link kaspersky-cyberstrikeai-schools-2026 and trendai-chinese-language-operators-used-cyberstrikeais-2026-10.
attacks.region_notes: No victim country is stated. Hong Kong and AS133199 are the server's hosting location and are not recorded as a target region.

attacks.name: SOCRadar XaocMail ClickFix delivers Phantom53 and HavoX, built with Claude Code

sources.title: XaocMail ClickFix Campaign Drops Phantom53 and HavoX Across Latin America, Asia, and Europe

attacks.ai_role_detail: SOCRadar found Claude Code project files, 143 numbered task markdown files, a 117 KB architecture note, and a Russian prompt that frames implant testing as an authorized red-team job.
attacks.technique_summary: SOCRadar Threat Research Unit (published Nov 13, 2026) describes a Russian-speaking operator chaining XaocMail, Phantom53, and HavoX (Havoc Demon). Preparation began in October 2025. Phishing tests and framework development continued in early 2026. The operation launched in August 2026 and was still active at publication. XaocMail, on 185.224.132.148:8585, builds per-victim document-sharing lures (Google Docs, Adobe Acrobat, Office365, SecuredDocs) and stores landing JSON in Cloudflare KV. Emails point at hxxps://securedoc.[subdomain].workers.dev/?id={linkId}. The ClickFix page offers three Win+R paths: a PowerShell DownloadString cradle, mshta against /h?id=X (an earlier ZIP of GUP.exe sideloading libcurl.dll), and msiexec /i .../m?id=X /qn, which SOCRadar calls the active path. The MSI impersonates names such as Visual Studio Tools, Python, or Node.js and drops Python 3.11 under a random directory in AppData or LocalAppData. A pythonw scheduled task runs the beacon every 12 minutes. A second task runs the watcher every 3 minutes. The beacon is a .pyd named like a real package (cv2.pyd, with PyInit_cv2, and the same pattern for numpy, PIL, and lxml). It beacons over DNS-over-HTTPS to Cloudflare, Google, and ControlD, encoding commands in AAAA records, with UDP/53 as a fallback, and a week-keyed SHA256 DGA on .xyz. CMD_WAKE writes an IPC file so the watcher reflectively loads an AES-GCM HavoX blob in memory. If the MSI is not elevated it can show a UAC prompt for a product-named task, and a separate payload uses fodhelper.exe registry hijacking. Payload aliases include a Level RMM drop from downloads.level.io and an AI-secret stealer covering Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, and other AI tools, plus password-manager, browser, SSH, git, wallet, and messaging collection. SOCRadar's AI evidence is on the operator side: .claude/settings.json, 143 numbered NNN-task-name.md files across adminka (25), implant_v3 (31), and implant_v4 (87), a 117 KB implant_v4/arch.md, and implant_v4/.tasks/prompts/noav-beacon-test.md, a Russian prompt for a claudeg5f-tmux Claude wrapper that tells the agent to install a test MSI on a VM named NoAV under an authorized red-team framing. HavoX's login panel and an exfiltration path are on 145.63.138.67. Almost a thousand personalized pages were identified. Named target countries are Brazil, Peru, India, Indonesia, and Spain, across technology, finance, education, government, logistics, and manufacturing. SOCRadar did not confirm attacker intent beyond the footholds.
attacks.initial_access: Spearphishing links from XaocMail to Cloudflare Worker ClickFix pages that ask the user to run msiexec, mshta, or a PowerShell cradle
ai_tooling_and_models: Claude Code (.claude/settings.json, numbered task files, claudeg5f-tmux prompt wrapper)
AI-secret stealer aimed at Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and Windsurf
other_tooling: Phantom53 DoH beacon and watcher (.pyd under pythonw.exe)
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Technology, finance, education, government, logistics, and manufacturing. Almost a thousand personalized lure pages. No organization names are listed here.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed Russian-speaking operator. SOCRadar does not name a country or a tracked cluster.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Almost a thousand personalized XaocMail pages. 143 Claude Code task files. implant_v4/arch.md is 117 KB. No victim-host count was published.
attacks.prevention_angle: Block ClickFix paste-and-run. Alert when explorer.exe starts msiexec.exe with a workers.dev URL, when mshta.exe fetches an HTTP URL, and when pythonw.exe runs a .pyw from AppData and loads a .pyd outside a normal Python install. Hunt scheduled tasks named like MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTask, OneDriveSyncTask, WindowsDefenderScheduledScan, OfficeBackgroundTaskHandler, or AdobeAcrobatUpdateTask with a short random suffix. Treat DoH from pythonw.exe to 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, or 76.76.2.11 as suspicious when paired with those tasks.
attacks.source_notes: Chain, timings, Claude Code artifacts, and IOCs are from the SOCRadar article. Operator mailbox addresses in that IOC table are omitted. Victim names and stolen-file contents are not included. The article lists additional MSI and payload hashes beyond the set below. Havoc is the public framework; HavoX is SOCRadar's name for this operator's Demon build.
attacks.region_notes: Brazil, Peru, India, Indonesia, and Spain are the countries SOCRadar names. The article also describes the set as Latin America, Asia, and Europe. Operator language is not a victim region.

attacks.name: Elastic REF3364 SANSAR takes over exposed Ray GPU hosts and hides utilization

sources.title: 0% GPU utilization: How SANSAR hides Linux cryptomining

attacks.ai_role_detail: The target is Ray, a distributed Python framework used for AI training and inference. The attacker is not described as using a model. The NVML wrapper is aimed at the GPU telemetry ML operators watch.
attacks.technique_summary: Elastic Security Labs (Salim Bitam, Nov 12, 2026) tracks REF3364. The Ray dashboard was bound to loopback, but the job agent was reachable from the internet and accepted unauthenticated Jobs API submissions. External probes appeared in the Ray logs on October 22, 2026. On October 24 a submitted job ran nvidia-smi and sent the GPU inventory out. On October 25 a Python reverse-shell job connected to an external listener under the account that owned the Ray session. The actor added an SSH key to that account's authorized_keys, obtained root, and staged SANSAR under /opt/vadi_ on three GPU hosts. SANSAR is a Rust orchestrator (v0.1.3) with Tor/Arti command and control and Lyrebird obfs4/WebTunnel. It supervises XMRig, stored as kurt, and SRBMiner-MULTI, stored as tilki (https://github.com/xmrig/xmrig and https://github.com/doktor83/SRBMiner-Multi). A replaced libnvidia-ml.so.1 wraps the real NVML library and reports GPU use as 0 percent, randomizes temperature between 36 and 46 C and power between 100 and 200 W, and filters process lists, so nvidia-smi and other NVML clients lie. An ftrace rootkit, acpi_thermal_mgr.ko, is built with DKMS, loaded through the initramfs, and hides processes, files, and sockets. A systemd backdoor named netns reads its command-and-control address from an Ethereum smart contract and connects on TCP 8080. Elastic publishes YARA rules for SANSAR and netns. Link shadowray-2-0-hijacks-exposed-ray-2025-11.
attacks.initial_access: Unauthenticated Ray Jobs API on an internet-reachable job agent
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Three GPU hosts running Ray. Elastic did not name the organizations.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: REF3364. Elastic does not attribute the activity to a named group or country.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Three GPU hosts. Activity from October 22 through October 25, 2026, from probe to persistent access.
attacks.prevention_angle: Do not expose the Ray job agent. Require authentication on the Jobs API. Alert on a Python reverse shell from the Ray account, a new authorized_keys entry, an out-of-tree kernel module, and a miner command line even when the binary is named kurt or tilki. Compare nvidia-smi with a second GPU telemetry source so a wrapped libnvidia-ml.so.1 cannot be the only reading.
attacks.source_notes: Dates, paths, component names, and the seven SHA-256 hashes are from the Elastic Security Labs article. The miners are renamed, so a rule that requires the process name xmrig or srbminer will miss kurt and tilki. The NVML change is a replaced libnvidia-ml.so.1, not an LD_PRELOAD or ld.so.preload edit, so those rules are not cited.
attacks.region_notes: Elastic did not name the countries of the GPU hosts.

attacks.name: Eye Security ARTEX intrusion from a PHP webshell to GitOps and CI runners

sources.title: Machine speed: how we defended against an AI-driven attack

attacks.ai_role_detail: Eye Security recovered ARTEX markers in pod names, files, data probes, and user agents during a multi-day incident at a payment and gift-card company. The agents adapted a rate-limit bypass in about three minutes.
attacks.technique_summary: Eye Security (Bas van den Berg, Nov 12, 2026) describes a multi-day ARTEX intrusion that started at a vulnerable custom PHP upload function. Uploads were extension-fuzzed (.phtml, .php5, .php7, .phar, .inc, .PHP) into webshells such as artx_s5.php and zzartx0000.php. The shell accepted header X-ARTX-KEY or parameter k, used key k=x9f3c2b7e, and returned ### ARTX-AGENT. Environment variables on the pod leaked API keys, and the first call with a stolen key landed within minutes. When a rate limiter engaged, the agents rewrote their client in about three minutes to rotate a spoofed client-IP header and peaked at over 9,000 requests a minute. After that path was blocked they used a pool of more than 17,000 residential proxies. They pulled Neo-reGeorg (https://github.com/L-codes/Neo-reGeorg) and changed it to keep state in the internal cache so it worked across load-balanced pods. Its default user agent is Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:38.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/38.0. With an engineer's Git hosting identity they changed the deployment repo so GitOps deployed attacker pods, including artx-pod and a privileged pod on a staging host. Deleting the pod brought it back within a second. From the privileged pod they broke out to the node with nsenter. Separately, Eye counted thirteen logins in under three minutes, one socket per login, asking a file-transfer server to forward Docker, containerd, CRI-O, lightweight Kubernetes, the system bus, the PHP worker pool, the process supervisor, and sshd. The server refused every one of those forwards. A CI app key from the secret store was used to register self-hosted GitHub runners named sink-*, re-registered about every eight minutes through the night. Backdoor admins looked like QA or audit accounts (qa_probe_*, qa.audit29a). In phpMyAdmin they used LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE into databases named artx_* and INTO OUTFILE write tests at /tmp/x.php5. The operators went after gift-card codes. Eye also publishes OSINT infrastructure from similar ARTEX activity: 207.5.195.93, artex.lol, staging.artex.lol, artex.tokena2b.top, artex.ok7777.eu.cc, artex.noog2infra.site, images tomicdd/artex and congdonglinux/artex, and callbacks on dnslog.cn, oast.me, and webhook.site. Data markers include ARTEX_WRITE_PROBE, ARTEX-PROBE-0001, ARTX_PERSIST_OK, and artex_control_marker_zz9q. Link srm-artex-ir-host-artifacts-2026-11, datadog-artex-aws-cognito-2026-11, arctic-wolf-antifox-iis-aws-2026-11, microsoft-artex-github-secrets-keyvault-2026-11, and badbyte-artex-backdoor-docker-2026-11.
attacks.initial_access: Vulnerable custom PHP upload function, then extension-fuzzed webshells
attacks.victims_and_sectors: A company running payment and gift-card services. Eye did not name the company.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Eye ties one address to public ARTEX reporting on payment-API abuse. No country is given.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Peak over 9,000 requests a minute. More than 17,000 residential proxy addresses. Thirteen socket-forward logins in under three minutes, all refused by the server. GitOps recreated a deleted attacker pod within a second. Runners were re-registered about every eight minutes.
attacks.prevention_angle: Block the published webshell names and the X-ARTX-KEY header. Alert on php-fpm or the web server spawning a shell, nsenter into the host PID namespace, a privileged pod, and a new self-hosted GitHub runner such as sink-*. Treat GitOps reconciliation as a persistence path: a deleted artx-pod that returns immediately is the deployment repo, not a restart.
attacks.source_notes: File names, the shell key, the request peak, the proxy count, the GitHub runner names, and the nsenter breakout are from the Eye Security incident write-up. 207.5.195.93 and the artex.* domains are in Eye's OSINT infrastructure list for similar ARTEX activity, not described as addresses observed inside this victim. Neo-reGeorg is tracked by LOTTunnels at https://lottunnels.github.io/lottunnels/Binaries/neo-regeorg/. The Sigma ReGeorg web-log rule requires a null user agent, and this tunnel used Firefox/38.0, so that rule is not cited.
attacks.region_notes: Eye did not name the victim's country. Infrastructure countries are not recorded as victim regions.

atlas_techniques.rationale: The operators deployed the ARTEX agent framework and Neo-reGeorg.
Initial access was a vulnerable PHP upload function turned into webshells.

attacks.name: FBI FLASH FaceStealer uses stolen webcam video and BlueNoroff deepfakes

sources.title: FBI FLASH AC-111226-MS: FaceStealer
Still in the Meeting: BlueNoroff Six Months On
Still in the Meeting: BlueNoroff Six Months On (white paper)
BlueNoroff uses ClickFix, fileless PowerShell, and AI-generated Zoom meetings
Inside a DPRK BlueNoroff ClickFix kit
Coverage of the FaceStealer disruption
FBI warns of North Korean fake Zoom calls

attacks.ai_role_detail: The FBI FLASH says the operators use what it calls super intelligence to make deepfake video of well-known crypto and web3 figures from public photos and video, and that stolen real footage is still most of the scheme. Arctic Wolf is the generator provenance: 122 assets from seven generators, identified from embedded tags and C2PA data rather than appearance. Grok Imagine and Google Generative AI were nearly two-thirds, with Wondershare AIGC, GPT-4o, GPT Image, and BytePlus ModelArk making up the rest.
attacks.technique_summary: FBI FLASH AC-111226-MS (Nov 12, 2026) describes FaceStealer, attributed to Sapphire Sleet / BlueNoroff / APT38 / UNC1069. The operators take over a victim's Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, or Discord account, read the chat history, and message contacts to catch up or talk investment. A Calendly invite sets the time. Shortly before the call, the link points at a typosquat such as uu01webzoom.us or teams.livemeet.us. The copycat Zoom or Teams page plays the trusted contact's stolen webcam recording, often next to other participants. A chat message says the target cannot be heard and walks them through an update, script, or terminal paste that installs a cookie harvester, keyloggers, a screen capturer, and a backdoor. The target's webcam is recorded from the moment the link opens and feeds the next round. The FBI says the group has begun using what it calls super intelligence to make deepfakes of crypto and web3 figures alongside stolen footage. Earlier in 2026 a maintainer of a widely downloaded JavaScript library ran the fix during a fake Teams call, and the operators then published malicious dependencies that were caught quickly. The FBI has also seen attempts against npm maintainers and, recently, Rust crate maintainers. Arctic Wolf's Nov 12 paper adds lures that end in a ClickFix command: NovaStream Player at vip.novaplayer.online (HTML SHA-256 ca14040cc48fbc3b00ea5f74e891266128f7bb3058be400782c5b08436f7668a), a Chrome PDF Viewer kit at chromeupdate.docdock.online and calendly.docdock.online, and calendly.idcheck.watch. The macOS idcheck command is curl piped to osacompile. The Windows cradle is curl piped to powershell -c with [Console]::In.ReadToEnd()|iex. Hosting includes Hostwinds 104.168.149.21, 104.168.149.182, and 104.168.149.230, and Petrosky 83.136.210.38 for docdock.online. Arctic Wolf's appendix lists 98 high-confidence domains. The domains below are that table plus the FBI examples and the lure hosts named in the paper. Link bluenoroff-uses-deepfaked-executives-fake-zoom-2025-06 and unc1069-gemini-deepfake-crypto-2025.
attacks.initial_access: Hijacked messenger accounts, then a typosquat Zoom or Teams page and a ClickFix paste
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Cryptocurrency and web3 individuals and companies, plus open-source maintainers. The FBI says the group stole more than $400 million in 18 months.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, APT38, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Stardust Chollima. FBI FLASH AC-111226-MS. Arctic Wolf independently attributes the activity to BlueNoroff.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: More than $400 million stolen in 18 months, per the FBI. Arctic Wolf: 122 AI-generated assets from seven generators, and 98 high-confidence domains on the Hostwinds cluster.
attacks.prevention_angle: Treat a meeting link that arrives in chat just before the call as hostile until the domain is the vendor's. Do not paste a command from a call. On Windows, hunt curl.exe piped into powershell with ReadToEnd and iex. On macOS, hunt curl and osacompile in the same command line. Block the domains and the four IPs below.
attacks.source_notes: The takeover loop, the two example typosquats, the deepfake statement, and the maintainer supply-chain note are from the FBI PDF. Generator counts, the ClickFix command lines, the Hostwinds and Petrosky addresses, the NovaStream hash, and the high-confidence domain table are from the Arctic Wolf white paper. The Sigma IEX rules require a space in '| iex' or 'iex ', and the published cradle is ReadToEnd()|iex with no space, so those rules are not cited. The osacompile run-only rule requires -x and -e, and the idcheck command uses osacompile -o, so that rule is not cited either. There is no attacker GitHub repository.
attacks.region_notes: North Korea is the actor origin from the FBI, not a victim region. Arctic Wolf's target countries are not listed as a closed set, so the entry uses Multiple regions.

sources.title: TypoPrompting: From AI Typos to Malware

attacks.ai_role_detail: Lookalike domains for AI products send visitors into ClickFix, a Store-signed browser hijacker, or a search-hijack extension. The AI products are the lure, not the operator.
attacks.technique_summary: Island (Oleg Zaytsev, Nov 12, 2026) traced 186 lookalike domains across 27 AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, and Cursor. A Nov 3, 2026 snapshot connected cloude.ai to a Windows ClickFix command and eight AI typos to an installer funnel. A Windows scan of cloude.ai went through xml.securetrackingnode.com/click to biomimicrydevtech.buzz (flow_id=81, bid about 0.0065 to 0.009) and then a random subdomain of blockchainfuturedev.buzz, which fingerprinted the browser and served a fake Cloudflare check. The recovered command was cmd /c curl.exe -fsL --ssl-no-revoke --retry 8 saving %TEMP%\W901.ps1 from 3112851459/985, then powershell -w h -nop -ep bypass -File that script. 3112851459 is 185.138.88.3 as a decimal integer. Pivoting the gate script hash found 550 scan records across 211 entry domains from April 2025 through November 2026, including lookalikes of banks, insurers, and enterprise software, plus Windows, macOS curl-to-zsh, and archive lures. Eight typos, including ckaude.ai, deepceek.com, copiot.com, elevenlebs.io, and vocie.ai, went through deezyj.com to fake Security Check pages that installed Net Guard, a Microsoft Store-signed Tauri app (publisher Myflixly App, product id 9MX3CH3BQ44Q, package family MyflixlyApp.NetGuard_k6q889pad57pt, analyzed 1.0.9.0). Island says the MSIX matches the Store hash and that buntai-sdk can change the default search engine, run JavaScript through DevTools Runtime.evaluate, and edit browser profiles. The same SDK is in Privacy Keeper 1.0.10.0 and MyFlixly Browser 1.0.10.0. The installer funnel spans 191 lander domains. preplexity.ai went to quickflashtool.com and a Chrome extension that sets the default search provider to find.flashysearches.com. It is one of 30 extensions from the same kit. Thirteen had been removed. The 17 still listed showed 972,000 declared users in total on November 3. Island says Socket's Oct 29, 2026 Searchjacked research lists 22 of the 30. An 81-domain portfolio including about 23 AI lookalikes ties to a11.click. Link anyrun-fake-ai-tools-2026-10.
attacks.initial_access: A mistyped AI domain is handed to a traffic-distribution system that selects a ClickFix command, a Store installer, or an extension page

attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Island ties an 81-domain portfolio to a11.click and shared affiliate keys. No country is stated.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: 186 lookalike domains, 27 AI brands, in the Nov 3, 2026 snapshot. 211 entry domains on the ClickFix gate. 972,000 declared users across 17 still-listed search extensions on Nov 3. Net Guard funnel about 1,437 source domains.
attacks.prevention_angle: Publish managed bookmarks for approved AI services. Alert when curl.exe writes a .ps1 and PowerShell starts with -w h and -ep bypass, including decimal hosts such as 3112851459. Do not treat a Microsoft Store signature as a reason to allow Net Guard package family MyflixlyApp.NetGuard_k6q889pad57pt. Enforce a managed search provider and block the extension IDs below.
attacks.source_notes: Counts, the ClickFix command, decimal IP 3112851459, package identifiers, and the 972,000-user figure are from Island. The article's appendix lists more lookalikes than the IOC set below. Link anyrun-fake-ai-tools-2026-10. Historical payloads on chatlgpt.com, midj0urney.org, and deepsek.icu are included only as Island states them.

attacks.name: Unit 42 CL-STA-1238 uses Cairn with Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek against semiconductor, defense, and civil-society targets

sources.title: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors
Cairn
GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold

attacks.ai_role_detail: CL-STA-1238 ran a customized Cairn fork so Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash or Pro planned and executed intrusion tasks. A Chinese authorization preamble told the model never to refuse.
attacks.technique_summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (published Nov 12, 2026) tracks CL-STA-1238, assessed with moderate confidence as China-nexus intelligence collection. From August through September 2026, Chinese-speaking operators used the open-source Cairn framework (https://github.com/oritera/Cairn) for 25 operations against at least 19 organizations and confirmed unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10. They paired Cairn with Zhipu GLM 5.2 (13 operations), DeepSeek V4 Flash (8), and DeepSeek V4 Pro (4), using the higher-tier Pro model for repeats against targets that resisted Flash. Each operation loaded a skill pack named AIScan Runner Skills, which Unit 42 says is not in upstream Cairn. A worker system-prompt preamble framed every Reason and Explore phase as authorized security testing, CTF, assessment, vulnerability research, or code audit and forbade refusal. Each operation also wrote AUTHORIZATION.md treating task creation as a client-approved engagement. Neither model refused that framing. Operators supplied a one-line goal and a root domain, and sometimes prior intelligence such as VPN gateway addresses, group names, and shared group passwords. Cairn then mapped the target, broke the goal into three to seven stages, and looped until the model judged the goal met, options exhausted, or the operator stopped it. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours. Confirmed outcomes include weak-password spraying that yielded dozens of valid credentials and non-public directory data at an industry standards body, plus an unauthenticated cloud-storage write that overwrote a live standards-ballot document; a brute-forced production credential at a semiconductor company followed by unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token; an unauthenticated account-creation bypass at a U.S. teachers' union that logged access to more than one million member records, roughly 31,000 CRM contacts, and staff password hashes; an open registration endpoint on a defense-policy identity platform exposing roughly 500 user records, including .mil and .gov accounts; and five further cases covering tens of thousands of content-management records, employee data at a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, roughly 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation manufacturer, and student data at an education nonprofit. Targeting concentrated on semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain (seven organizations), defense and defense policy (three, including a space technology company, a defense-analytics vendor, and a policy think tank), and human rights and civil society (four, including a Canadian human-rights body, a U.S. teachers' union, a science-policy advocacy group, and an education nonprofit). Unit 42 assesses a single operator or small team. The exploited flaws were known classes: authentication bypasses, insecure direct object references, mass-assignment privilege escalation, weak and default credentials, exposed cloud APIs, and dated public CVEs. Infrastructure: Cairn hosting 154.44.31.4 (Hong Kong, AS979, NetLab Global) and egress and staging 82.29.129.54 (United States, AS142036, Hosteons Pte. Ltd.). Link cairn-norforge-2026-10 and cert-in-crafty-falcon-bfsi-2026-11.
attacks.initial_access: Operator-supplied root domain, sometimes with pre-gathered VPN gateways, group names, and shared passwords. Cairn then used authentication bypasses, weak or default credentials, insecure object references, and exposed cloud APIs.
ai_tooling_and_models: AIScan Runner Skills pack (not in upstream Cairn)
attacks.victims_and_sectors: At least 19 organizations in semiconductor and advanced manufacturing, defense and defense policy, and human rights and civil society. Confirmed access or data retrieval at 10.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: CL-STA-1238. Unit 42 assesses moderate confidence of China-nexus intelligence collection from Chinese tasking and authorization files, exclusive use of Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, and the target set.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: 25 operations, at least 19 organizations, confirmed unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10. Thirteen operations on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash, four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. One organization exceeded one million member records. Operations lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours.
attacks.prevention_angle: Treat agent-driven scanning as ordinary vulnerability volume, not a new exploit class. Remove weak and default credentials, close unauthenticated registration and cloud-storage writes, and patch known public-facing flaws. Block the two published IPs. Do not treat a same-/24 scan lead as this cluster without Unit 42's indicators.
attacks.source_notes: Counts, models, the AIScan Runner Skills pack, the authorization preamble, the confirmed outcomes, and the two IPs are from the Unit 42 article. 154.44.31.104 was described as another live Cairn panel in the same /24 as the controller 154.44.31.4, attributed to a Censys observation. It is not in the Unit 42 indicator list, and no public Censys report naming that address was available to confirm it. It is an unconfirmed lead only and is not an IOC. Cairn is open source, so an exposed panel is not by itself this cluster. Link cairn-norforge-2026-10, the cairn tool page, and cert-in-crafty-falcon-bfsi-2026-11. No victim organization names are repeated beyond the sector descriptions Unit 42 published. The 16 November 2026 GTIG tracker says GTIG observed Cairn used in intrusion activity against targets including a US aerospace organization. GTIG does not name CL-STA-1238, does not give indicators, and does not say that intrusion is this cluster. The note is recorded here because this is the catalog's Cairn intrusion entry. frameworks remains cairn.
attacks.region_notes: Named targets include U.S. defense-policy organizations, a U.S. teachers' union, and a Canadian human-rights body. Other organizations' countries were not stated. Hong Kong and the U.S. egress host are infrastructure, not victim regions, so the entry uses Multiple regions.

attacks.name: Barracuda - an unretired vendor cloud key used in an ARTEX-style intrusion

sources.title: Forty-four hours: Anatomy of a machine-speed intrusion
Barracuda XDR integration credentials
Barracuda links cloud breach to ARTEX AI-powered cyberattack
Barracuda hacked amid surge in ARTEX-powered cyberattacks
FBI FLASH-20261113-001 (CSA 261113): Threat overview of ARTEX. Does not name Barracuda.

attacks.ai_role_detail: Barracuda matches resource names, probe names, order of operations, and built-in credential and wallet hunting to ARTEX. The tool was not recovered, and the match does not identify the operator.
attacks.technique_summary: Barracuda (Arve Kjoelen, CISO; blog Nov 11, 2026, after a Trust Center advisory on Nov 10) describes a cloud intrusion that used a valid access key the company had given a third-party AI vendor and never retired. In October the vendor's development environment was compromised. The Trust Center says the key was stored in a configuration file in that vendor's GitHub repository; other Barracuda credentials in the same file had already expired or were later revoked. First use was Nov 1, 2026 at 04:33 UTC. Within minutes the caller mapped what the key could reach and read secret stores, including AWS access keys and Azure service principal secrets. It decrypted infrastructure-as-code state files and pulled credentials from instance metadata services and Kubernetes service accounts. Over the next day each secret opened the next system: cloud accounts, then a data analytics system, then a source-code access token, then Kubernetes clusters. On Nov 2, in under four hours, short-lived branches were pushed to a handful of repositories so a build workflow printed the build system's secrets into the job log. The secrets were encoded so the log's usual masking would not hide them. Where a shell was obtained, commands searched for environment variables named WALLET, MNEMONIC, SEED, and PRIV, Ethereum keystore files, extended private keys, seed-phrase files, and Kubernetes secrets with wallet-related names. Barracuda says no wallet material was on those systems. For persistence, a container mounted one node's filesystem read-only and harvested that node's credentials. An attempt to create a new administrative cloud identity was blocked. About 10 cloud accounts were touched in roughly 44 hours. Last activity was Nov 2 at 23:31 UTC. An engineer noticed unusual activity on Nov 4, the same day the vendor reported its own incident, and the container was removed that evening Pacific time. Resources were labeled with the letter i followed by digits and no human-readable words. Barracuda says those labels, the probe names, the order of operations, and the built-in credential and wallet routines match ARTEX (https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX). Because many groups use ARTEX, the match describes the method, not a named actor. Barracuda found no direct evidence that Barracuda Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint integration credentials were viewed, but logging was not detailed enough to rule it out, and those customers were asked to rotate them. ATT&CK coverage in the write-up is T1552.005 (cloud instance metadata), T1078.004 (valid cloud accounts), T1610 (deploy container), and T1611 (escape to host via the mounted node filesystem). FBI FLASH-20261113-001, CSA 261113 (https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2026/261113.pdf), is a general ARTEX overview and does not name Barracuda.
attacks.initial_access: Valid cloud access key issued to a third-party AI vendor, left unretired, and later found in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository after that vendor's development environment was compromised in October
ai_tooling_and_models: ARTEX (https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX); the tool was not recovered
other_tooling: Cloud secret stores, infrastructure-as-code state files, instance metadata, and Kubernetes service accounts
Short-lived Git branches that triggered a build workflow and printed secrets into job logs
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Barracuda cloud environment, including a data analytics system, source-code access, Kubernetes clusters, and the system that stores Barracuda XDR customer integration credentials. Barracuda says it found no direct evidence those customer credentials were viewed.
attacks.region_notes: Barracuda is the named victim. The blog does not state which cloud region the accounts ran in, and it does not name the vendor's country.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Barracuda ties the labels, probe names, order of operations, and credential and wallet hunting to ARTEX, and says that match does not identify the operator. The wallet searches are the evidence for a financial motive. AI-service credentials were also in reach; Barracuda does not claim they were the goal.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: About 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours, from Nov 1 04:33 UTC to Nov 2 23:31 UTC. Detected Nov 4, after the activity had stopped.
attacks.prevention_angle: Retire third-party cloud keys when the work ends, and prefer short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials. Do not leave one secret able to read the next store, the source-code token, and the cluster credentials. Alert on bulk secret reads, instance-metadata credential requests, Kubernetes secret lists, a new pod with a hostPath mount, and a new cloud administrator identity. Treat a short-lived branch whose build log prints secrets, especially encoded values that slip past log masking, as a credential-exposure event. Practice rotating every secret in reach, including customer integration keys, without waiting for proof they were read.
attacks.source_notes: Times, the GitHub configuration-file detail, the wallet variable names, the read-only host mount, the blocked administrator identity, and the account count are from the Barracuda blog and Trust Center advisory. The community ARTEX fork is https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX. FBI FLASH-20261113-001 does not name Barracuda; it is cited only so that gap is explicit. Link chainstack-intruder-reached-production-user-password-2026-11, datadog-artex-aws-cognito-2026-11, microsoft-artex-github-secrets-keyvault-2026-11, and eye-security-artex-gitops-2026-11.

Secrets were carried out by follow-on use of stolen keys and by a build log that printed encoded secret values.

attacks.name: Huntress SCKit installs rogue ScreenConnect clients; RelayTrap source looks LLM-written
attacks.researcher: Ben Nahorney, Susannah Matt, Lindsey O'Donnell-Welch

sources.title: SCKit Worm Installs Rogue ScreenConnect Clients and Session Cookie Relays Across Hundreds of Endpoints
New worm-like SCKit malware targets MSPs in ScreenConnect attacks
ScreenConnect attack: SCKit

attacks.ai_role_detail: Huntress Figure 6 says the RelayTrap C# source appears to have been generated by an LLM, based on detailed comments that explain what the code is intended to do. BleepingComputer reports the same inference. No prompts were published. The schema has no inferred value, so this is recorded as vendor-asserted.
attacks.technique_summary: Huntress (Ben Nahorney, Susannah Matt, Lindsey O'Donnell-Welch; published Nov 11, 2026, updated Nov 13) observed Run commands on cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels installing rogue ScreenConnect clients. On Nov 11, from about 17:47 UTC, at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations were hit in about 90 minutes. ScreenConnect 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783 were affected. Huntress ties the activity to the third-party RMM+ extension, versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32: if the access key was never set, the extension accepted a blank key, bypassing ScreenConnect user accounts, roles, and MFA. Commands showed up as RMM+ with no matching login. ConnectWise said it had disabled five extensions (Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link) across more than 400 partner environments and had not yet identified an initial access vector when the Nov 11 advisory posted. The Run command, as SYSTEM, downloaded an attacker ScreenConnect installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi, installed it silently, and wrote C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-run.bat. The dropper fetches sckit-decoder.ps1 and a kit keyed by the Windows UUID. Components extract to C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap. TrapWatch.ps1 runs as SYSTEM, compiles RelayTrap.cs into a host-specific RelayTrap.exe, and creates a scheduled task named TrapWatch that runs every 10 seconds. The legitimate ScreenConnect client is stopped and set to manual start. Huntress Figure 6 says the RelayTrap C# source appears to have been generated by an LLM because of detailed source comments explaining intent. A separate path, seen in the kit and not observed succeeding, steals the technician .aspxauth cookie with sqlite3.exe and tries to push WithUninstall.ps1 through the Shared Toolbox. On Nov 13 at 16:12 UTC Huntress saw another spike, 205 hosts across 41 organizations, with the client hosted at 185.241.211.197 and an installer URL ending in c=ExploitedNOTUSA. Huntress also saw c=Exploited529 and c=Exploited809. One incident used a self-hosted RMM+ plugin, a netsh portproxy from 127.0.0.1:88 to 185.241.211.197:80, and a service named Windows Update Agent running UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe from C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\. ConnectWise also pointed on-premises partners at ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later for CVE-2026-84869, a separate client file-transfer flaw. Huntress does not say this wave exploited that flaw. Blackpoint Cyber (Sam Decker, Nevan Beal) says RelayTrap.cs is compiled on the endpoint by TrapWatch.ps1, not shipped as a precompiled binary. When a technician connects, the replacement Guest sends TransferFilesMessage FileAction.Run after a 2.5 second delay, which is the CVE-2026-84869 file-transfer-back path. Blackpoint's test against a current ScreenConnect Host queued the transfer on the Guest, and the Host did not request or run the payload. They report no successful technician compromise. Primary panel indicators include sc.payproofkit.com (155.94.150.39) and 185.99.255.28.
attacks.initial_access: Blank access key on RMM+ 1.0.31 or 1.0.32, then ScreenConnect Run Command as SYSTEM. ConnectWise had not identified a single initial-access vector in the Nov 11 advisory.
ai_tooling_and_models: RelayTrap.cs, which Huntress says appears LLM-generated from its explanatory comments
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Organizations using Huntress and ScreenConnect. 48 organizations on Nov 11 and 41 on Nov 13. Sectors were not named.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Huntress and ConnectWise describe the activity. No country is stated. Participant name Addmin and client IDs 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091 were published.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Nov 11: at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations in about 90 minutes. Nov 13: 205 hosts across 41 organizations. ConnectWise disabled the listed extensions across more than 400 partner environments. One panel parameter reached Exploited809 (190 downstream clients on one panel).
attacks.prevention_angle: Disable RMM+ 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 where the access key was left blank, including on-premises ScreenConnect. Do not triage a suspect host over ScreenConnect. Remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch task, C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap, and sckit files under %TEMP%. Hunt msiexec installs of ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi or UpdateConnect.ClientSetup.msi with c=Exploited. Block 185.99.255.28 and 185.241.211.197.
attacks.source_notes: Counts, the blank-key behavior, Figure 6's LLM comment, paths, and IOCs are from the Huntress article, including the Nov 13 update. BleepingComputer reports the same LLM-looking comments. The console-takeover and Shared Toolbox spread were recovered from the kit and were not seen succeeding. Blackpoint's patched-host test is the source for the 2.5 second TransferFilesMessage and the result that a current Host did not fetch the payload. Additional acknowledged contributors include John Hammond, Tanner Filip, Tyler Marzen, Austin Worline, Ethan Williams, Sharon Martin, Ben Bernstein, Andrew Brandt, Jamie Levy, Max Rogers, Aaron Deal, and Mendy Green. File hashes are weak because scripts are rebuilt per host. ScreenConnect is tracked by LOLRMM at https://lolrmm.io/tools/screenconnect.
attacks.region_notes: Huntress did not name the countries of the affected organizations.

The Splunk on-the-fly csc rule also requires /noconfig, /fullpaths, and a response file, which the write-up does not show.
