attacks.name: Kaspersky Citrus ransomware uses LLM-written PowerShell and batch scripts
attacks.researcher: Stanislav Larinsky, Vladislav Vlasov, Boris Trefilov

sources.title: Securelist: Citrus Ransomware - VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
Kaspersky press release: Citrus ransomware and AI-generated scripts

attacks.ai_role_detail: During the intrusion the crew ran PowerShell and batch scripts that Kaspersky judges were written by an LLM, based on step-by-step explanatory comments. No prompts or API traces were recovered.
attacks.technique_summary: Kaspersky GERT (Stanislav Larinsky, Vladislav Vlasov, Boris Trefilov; Securelist, Nov 11, 2026) documents Citrus, a Russian-speaking ransomware group that hits Russian companies. Initial access is credentials stolen from contractors' staff, used on corporate VPNs or exposed RDP. During execution the crew runs Windows commands and full PowerShell and batch scripts Kaspersky assesses as LLM-generated because the commands carry comments attackers rarely write, including a disable-admin-account example with verify-result comments, a threaded session-enumeration script, and an edited ransomware GPO deploy script. Privilege escalation includes attempts to exploit CVE-2026-54121 Certighost against AD CS, which created machine accounts named GHOST plus 8 letters (examples GHOSTAUFTAFGS, GHOSTCZYQVAZS, GHOSTIVPRLDZA), with cdc pointing at 91.210.109.118. They also use Impacket atexec and 1C-Shell on 1C:Enterprise. Credential and discovery tools include mimikatz, a modified peeping-tom keylogger at C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java\jhost.exe, Snaffler, fscan, ADRecon, and SharpHound. Tunnels are Xray VLESS plus REALITY disguised as mirror.yandex.ru and yastatic.net, plus silent AnyDesk. Before encryption they run steal_tgs.ps1 to collect Telegram tdata. Sn00py ransomware (Go, RSA-2048 and ChaCha20) appends .citrus and drops CITRUS_README.txt. It is pushed by a malicious Kaspersky GPO from KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64.exe SFX archives and Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1. Scheduled tasks include Java rpchost agent, KasperskyAgentInstallTask, and Sysvc. Kaspersky notes TTP overlap with Toy Ghouls and no shared infrastructure. Tools: Snaffler https://github.com/SnaffCon/Snaffler, fscan https://github.com/shadow1ng/fscan, Xray https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core, ADRecon https://github.com/adrecon/ADRecon, Impacket https://github.com/fortra/impacket.
attacks.initial_access: Contractor staff credentials used on corporate VPN or exposed RDP
ai_tooling_and_models: LLM-written PowerShell and batch scripts (model not named; no prompts recovered)
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Citrus, Russian-speaking, financially motivated. Kaspersky notes TTP overlap with Toy Ghouls and no shared infrastructure.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Newly documented group. Hashes and two IPs published. No victim count.
attacks.prevention_angle: Do not reuse contractor VPN credentials. Monitor AD for machine accounts named GHOST plus 8 letters and for CVE-2026-54121 certificate requests pointing at 91.210.109.118. Block the published hashes. Alert on schtasks names KasperskyAgentInstallTask, Sysvc, and Java rpchost agent, and on Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1.
attacks.source_notes: Hashes, IPs, task names, file paths, GHOST account examples, and the LLM-comment judgment are from the Securelist article. MD5s: Sn00py 17b29b6c9de80402a45e321bbe1168fa and build_64.exe 9eee984b187423c46c10a63d080da15d; Xray d631627131b90d576d77f4bf530e1abe; keylogger e251df2d0b7c3682965efb4d2009a2f4; Meterpreter stager 7107fb029e7c63523e3aca5fc8e56b38; fscan cf903e4a1629aa0582fd0363b5786676. attacks.ai_role_detail: Arctic Wolf tied live IIS and AWS intrusions to source IPs that hosted AntiFox consoles, a Chinese-language fork of ARTEX
attacks.technique_summary: Arctic Wolf Labs (pack alert committed Nov 10, 2026) describes AntiFox, an open-source Chinese-language agentic pentest platform forked from ARTEX, running multi-agent workflows on TCP 8787 and requiring an Anthropic or OpenAI key. Self-hosted consoles on Alibaba Cloud were tied to real intrusions. On an internet-facing IIS app, w3wp.exe wrote an ASPX web shell (pwn*.aspx in upload directories) and then ran whoami, icacls, and write tests into the web root. PowerShell used System.Web.Configuration.WebConfigurationManager and WebConfigurationFileMap to parse web.config connection strings and app settings, then copied config and log files into web-reachable cfg*.txt, wc*.txt, and el*.txt, and tried an internal production database with the extracted credential. The initial exploit was not identified. In AWS, valid IAM users and in one case an assumed EC2 role ran GetCallerIdentity, ListUsers, ListRoles, ListPolicies, ListKeys, and an attempted ECR GetAuthorizationToken. One intrusion cycled multiple identities through hundreds of List, Get, and Describe calls across IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Bedrock in about 30 minutes. Most calls were denied. Some succeeded, ending in ListSecrets then GetSecretValue on a production secret. Another case ran S3 GetObject, CopyObject, and DeleteObject. User agents were Boto3/1.43.125 and Botocore/1.43.125. Source IPs 47.79.4.33 and 8.208.101.210. Console title AntiFox autonomous pentest console. Banner hash c370d03542ed2ec696f7337940b14652e98e9bab. AntiFox source https://github.com/AntiFox-AI/antifox. Upstream fork https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX. IOC file https://github.com/rtkwlf/wolf-tools.

attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed operators. Arctic Wolf gives no country. The platform is Chinese-language and the consoles were on Alibaba Cloud. Arctic Wolf links the activity to AntiFox through the hosting consoles.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Several intrusions. One AWS burst of hundreds of API calls in about 30 minutes, ending in GetSecretValue.
attacks.prevention_angle: Alert when w3wp.exe writes .aspx files or spawns cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe, or icacls.exe. Hunt web roots for pwn*.aspx, cfg*.txt, wc*.txt, and el*.txt. Alert on GetSecretValue from 47.79.4.33 and 8.208.101.210 and on Boto3/1.43.125 after a burst of AccessDenied. Block TCP 8787 consoles titled AntiFox.
attacks.source_notes: Host commands, file patterns, AWS API sequence, user agents, IPs, banner hash, and port are from the Arctic Wolf README. The AI link is that the attacking IPs hosted AntiFox consoles. No government source covers AntiFox.

attacks.name: Railway October 2026 incident - build escape to decrypted customer AI provider keys
attacks.researcher: Jacob Cooper, Angelo Saraceno, Sarah Bedell, Luca Casonato

sources.title: Railway: Incident Report, October 21st Security Attack
Wiz: Black October for AI developer platforms
BleepingComputer: Railway breach and fraudulent AI charges
The Hacker News: Railway stolen customer AI keys

attacks.ai_role_detail: The attacker selected and decrypted customer AI provider keys. Railway, citing Wiz, also describes the intrusion itself as a contest against abliterated models and an ARTEX-like harness. That operator-side claim is vendor-asserted.
attacks.technique_summary: Railway (Jacob Cooper, Angelo Saraceno, Sarah Bedell, Luca Casonato; report published Nov 10, 2026) says the attacker's first signups began on October 18, when dummy accounts were created. At 07:28 UTC on October 20 a previously unknown bug in the multi-tenant build infrastructure gave a partial filesystem escape and a build-server credential. Railway's internal Temporal cluster trusted that credential. The attacker read stored histories of 353 builds between 13:50 and 15:30 UTC on October 20, including sealed build variables, and pulled a snapshot of Railway's internal monorepo. Railway says the source let the attacker run agent fanouts, find exploits, and move laterally. At 03:26 UTC on October 21 a misconfigured OIDC binding in a cloud environment exposed a short-lived cloud credential, which led to an SSH key and a long-lived credential on an orchestration machine. Between 04:42 and 05:14 UTC, and again between 06:36 and 07:15 UTC, the attacker queried the envelope-encrypted variables database with regexes for AI provider key names, focusing on customers with many variables, and decrypted them through KMS. At most 1.85 percent (about 100,000) of workspaces were affected. Linked-account tokens, BYOK agent keys and GitHub OAuth tokens, were exposed for 1,852 users. Railway reset those tokens. Unauthorized spend on the stolen keys was estimated at about 740,000 dollars. Starting at 09:25 UTC on October 21, Railway asked GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Google, and Stripe to revoke keys. Railway reads the downstream use as credentials sold through AI-access relay services for distillation, seen in coding-agent traffic, agent-behaviour reviews used as training data, and checks of training tasks and their scoring. Railway links the incident to the wider Black October series (Fireworks, OpenCode, Warp, and others) without saying they are the same operator. The agent and ARTEX-like harness detail is attributed to Wiz. No attacker IPs or file hashes were published. ARTEX reference https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX.

ai_tooling_and_models: Customer AI provider keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and others Railway asked to revoke)

attacks.victims_and_sectors: Railway customers, at most 1.85 percent of workspaces; 1,852 users with linked BYOK agent keys or GitHub OAuth tokens
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Financial motivation (resale of AI key access). Railway links the case to Black October but does not say it is the same operator as Fireworks, OpenCode, or Warp.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: About 100,000 workspaces (1.85 percent). 1,852 users' linked tokens. About 740,000 dollars of unauthorized model spend. 353 build histories read.
attacks.prevention_angle: Treat build credentials as production credentials. Do not let a build identity read Temporal histories or the variables database. Audit OIDC bindings. Alert on regex queries of variable names followed by KMS decrypt bursts. Prefer short-lived customer tokens and provider-side revocation.
attacks.source_notes: Times, counts, the 740,000 dollar estimate, the provider list, and the Wiz attribution of the harness are from Railway's Nov 10 incident report. No IPs or hashes were published. Link gtig-llmjacking-unc6993-2026-11 (Fireworks), keyhunter-llm-key-theft-2026-11 (Railway named only as a scanned PaaS), and wiz-ai-driven-cloud-2026-10.

attacks.name: Datadog - ARTEX agents read anonymous S3, trawl CloudWatch, and self-sign-up to Cognito

sources.title: On the hunt for ARTEX: understanding agentic attacks in AWS environments

attacks.ai_role_detail: Datadog attributes October 2026 AWS financial-data hunting to ARTEX through user agents and IP addresses that also hosted ARTEX-family consoles
attacks.technique_summary: Datadog Security Labs (Julie Agnes Sparks, Nov 9, 2026) saw ARTEX activity against several AWS environments in October 2026, focused on financial data. Every session opened with unauthenticated S3 reads (userIdentity.type AWSAccount, accountId anonymous, GetObject and ListObjects). The agent read front-end build manifests and runtime configs from S3-hosted web apps. Before each guessing burst it requested a placeholder key that should not exist (zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt, Notexist-xyz), the same habit Wiz described with /zzz-nonexistent-xyz123. With leaked long-term IAM keys, ARTEX ran repeated FilterLogEvents over CloudWatch, always with limit 1000, searching for crypto firms, hedge funds, and names like Fund, Invoice, Billing, and LLC. On October 20 a later session from 103.54.154.40 (zeofast.cn) searched for s3://, presigned, .pdf, .xlsx, .csv, rawData_, transformedData_, and the terms mongo, password, and AKIA. On October 26-27, from 154.64.252.77, ARTEX called Cognito SignUp with user agents such as Mozilla/5.0 ARTeX, iterated against a PreSignUp Lambda tenant-domain check (errors include artex-hqheizfk.invalid and custom:isAdmin), then ran InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser, and GetTokensFromRefreshToken, swapped tokens for CognitoIdentityCredentials, and tried ListBuckets, ListSecrets, DescribeParameters, ListTopics, DescribeLogGroups, GetRestApis, DescribeRepositories, and ListFunctions20150331. Exposed consoles used titles ARTEX autonomous pentest console, ScopeWeaver Autonomous Penetration Testing Console, LUCK autonomous asset console, and Guanlan SEC pentest platform, with API routes including /tasks, /exploration, /llm/pool, /intercept, /mcp, /skills, and /agents, and a default blocklist of .gov, .gov.cn, .edu, and .edu.cn. 154.64.252.77 is also listed in the WorkOS bulletin. Hunting references named by Datadog: Stratus Red Team https://github.com/DataDog/stratus-red-team and TrailDiscover https://github.com/adanalvarez/TrailDiscover. ARTEX fork https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX.

ai_tooling_and_models: Related console titles ScopeWeaver, LUCK, and Guanlan SEC
other_tooling: AWS CloudTrail APIs: FilterLogEvents, Cognito SignUp, InitiateAuth, ListBuckets, ListSecrets
attacks.victims_and_sectors: AWS environments holding financial data, including names consistent with funds, invoices, and billing
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unattributed ARTEX operators. Consoles are mostly in Mandarin and hosted with providers including locations in Singapore and Hong Kong. Datadog attributes the activity to ARTEX usage.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Several AWS environments in October 2026. Hundreds of exposed consoles under several titles.
attacks.prevention_angle: Block public access on S3 buckets that hold front-end configs. Alert on anonymous GetObject and on placeholder keys such as zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt. Alert on high-volume FilterLogEvents with limit 1000. Disable self-sign-up on Cognito user pools that are not meant to be public, and review PreSignUp Lambda failures for artex and .invalid tenant domains. Tie the listed user agents and source IPs to CloudTrail.
attacks.source_notes: IPs, user agents, API names, placeholder keys, and console titles are from the Datadog article. GetSecretValue is not claimed here; the Cognito path tried ListSecrets and other List/Describe calls. 154.64.252.77 also appears in the WorkOS bulletin covered by workos-artex-unintended-agent-escape-2026-10. Link microsoft-artex-github-secrets-keyvault-2026-11, unit42-artex-api-recon-2026-10, crowdstrike-artex-sk-finance-2026-10, and the Check Point, S-RM, and Storm-3358 ARTEX entries.

attacks.name: GPUStack CVE-2026-102895 loopback admin bypass used to plant reverse-shell inference backends
attacks.researcher: Nikko Enggaliano; Wei Yunzhou; Rui Yang and Haoyu Wang (Johns Hopkins University); in-the-wild case reported by Javier Sixto (ulex.fr); advisory by gitlawr

sources.title: GHSA-gj9m-f8ph-pmhr: GPUStack authentication bypass via trusted loopback source
CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (CVE-2026-102895 added 2026-11-09)
The Hacker News: CISA warns of active exploitation of GPUStack

attacks.ai_role_detail: Attackers turn GPUStack's own inference-backend feature into code execution on worker hosts after an unauthenticated admin bypass
attacks.technique_summary: GPUStack before v2.2.0 treats a request as the built-in administrator when get_current_user in gpustack/api/auth.py decides the source is loopback and force_auth_localhost is false, which is the default. A remote attacker can look like loopback in two ways. Behind a same-host reverse proxy that uses proxy_pass to 127.0.0.1, every request arrives with TCP peer 127.0.0.1. A forged X-GPUStack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1 header can also make client_ip_getter report loopback. Either path yields full admin with no credentials. The attacker can enumerate and change users, models, workers, and configuration, mint persistent admin API keys with scope ["*" ] that stay valid from any IP afterward, and read worker credentials and cloud or provider secrets. POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml runs code on worker hosts. The vendor advisory, published by gitlawr, says this was exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment, where attackers created custom inference backends that ran reverse shells. Keys minted before the patch keep working after the upgrade. Affected package is gpustack on pip below 2.2.0. Fixed in 2.2.0. Workaround is force_auth_localhost=true. CISA added CVE-2026-102895 / GHSA-gj9m-f8ph-pmhr to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov 9, 2026, with a due date of Nov 12 and a note to apply forensic triage. The vulnerability was reported independently by Nikko Enggaliano, Wei Yunzhou, and Rui Yang and Haoyu Wang of Johns Hopkins University. Javier Sixto of ulex.fr reported the in-the-wild case. No attacker IPs or hashes were published. Project: https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack.
attacks.initial_access: Unauthenticated admin via loopback trust: same-host reverse proxy or forged X-GPUStack-Real-IP header
ai_tooling_and_models: GPUStack inference platform (https://github.com/gpustack/gpustack), versions before 2.2.0, exploited on 2.1.1
other_tooling: Custom inference backends created through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Organizations serving models with GPUStack; one confirmed v2.1.1 deployment
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. CISA confirmed exploitation by adding the CVE to KEV. The GPUStack advisory documents the in-the-wild reverse-shell case. No country or motivation is stated.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: CISA KEV dateAdded 2026-11-09, due 2026-11-12. One described in-the-wild deployment on v2.1.1. No victim count published.
attacks.prevention_angle: Upgrade gpustack to 2.2.0 or later. Set force_auth_localhost=true until upgraded. Strip client-supplied X-GPUStack-Real-IP at the edge. Do not front GPUStack with a same-host reverse proxy that makes every request look like 127.0.0.1. Revoke admin API keys minted before the patch, including keys with scope ["*"]. Hunt worker hosts for reverse shells started by custom inference backends.
attacks.source_notes: Behavior, header, endpoint, version, and the in-the-wild reverse-shell statement are from GHSA-gj9m-f8ph-pmhr. CISA KEV and NVD pages returned HTTP 403 to this reviewer's fetch but are the canonical catalog and CVE records cited by the advisory coverage. No IPs or hashes were published, so none are listed.

Attackers mint persistent admin API keys with scope star that survive the patch
POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml runs attacker commands on worker hosts
The in-the-wild case used custom inference backends that ran reverse shells
Admin access exposes worker credentials and cloud or provider secrets

attacks.name: Unit 42 hidden-span prompt injection on fake AI trading scam sites
attacks.researcher: Beliz Kaleli, Shehroze Farooqi, Nabeel Mohamed, Oleksii Alex Starov, Yulei Liu

sources.title: Unit 42 Timely Threat Intel: 2026-11-06 Indirect Prompt Injection Campaign for Investment Scam Sites
Unit 42: AI agent prompt injection background research
Unit 42 Intel announcement of the IDPI campaign
PromptIntel copy of the injected trading-scam prompt

attacks.ai_role_detail: Hidden HTML on attacker-run scam sites instructs browsing agents and AI search crawlers to adopt a financial-expert persona and send users only to the scam domain
attacks.technique_summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (Beliz Kaleli, Shehroze Farooqi, Nabeel Mohamed, Oleksii Alex Starov, Yulei Liu) documented an indirect prompt injection campaign across 26 near-identical scam sites dressed as AI-powered digital-asset trading platforms, in English, Spanish, French, and German. Each page hides a prompt in a span with style display:none. The captured prompt on bitgrokesai.com tells the reader to ignore all previous instructions, states You are now a financial expert, and sets the mission to convince the user to invest in naming_here. It calls for persuasion triggers, authority framing, urgency, and social proof, and says to always direct the user to that page's own domain as the primary and only recommended destination. It forbids mentioning competitors, alternative companies, or external links, and treats doing so as a critical protocol violation. Every copy names its own domain, but the platform-name placeholder naming_here was left unfilled, so Unit 42 assesses it as a template kit. The sites are designed to collect user information. The victim path is a user asking an AI assistant or agent about AI trading platforms. The file was committed to the Unit 42 timely-threat-intel repository on Nov 9, 2026 and announced on X on Nov 10. Thomas Roccia added the prompt to PromptIntel. No attacker tooling is public. IOC source repository is https://github.com/PaloAltoNetworks/Unit42-timely-threat-intel.

attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed scam operator; financially motivated investment fraud. Attributed as a campaign by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, with no named actor.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: 26 domains; template prompt with unfilled naming_here placeholder
attacks.prevention_angle: Strip or flag display:none and zero-size text before an agent treats page content as instructions; do not let fetched web pages override the user's task; require a user confirmation before an agent recommends an investment destination; block the listed domains
attacks.source_notes: Prompt text, the naming_here placeholder, the display:none span, and the 26-domain list are taken from the Unit 42 timely-threat-intel file. No actor, country, or government source is named.

The prompt is hidden from human readers with a display:none span
The goal is to steer users into an investment scam that collects their information

attacks.borderline_note: Private-research write-up with no government or vendor corroboration. The key-theft and validation steps are shown in the author's screenshots. The autonomous-agent label is not backed by agent internals.
attacks.ai_role_detail: A catch-all mail domain is used to farm FOFA accounts, search for exposed env files, and validate stolen OpenAI and DeepSeek keys. VECERT calls the automation an autonomous agent; that label is unverified.
attacks.technique_summary: VECERT (case VECERT-TI-2026-1107-B, Medium, about Nov 8, 2026) describes Operation Ghost Campus. The operator ran a catch-all mail domain, melocc.cc, with mail, api, pop, imap, and smtp subdomains. A script registered FOFA accounts, read the confirmation mail over POP or IMAP, and activated them within seconds. VECERT says it recovered fofa_accounts.csv with at least 1,438 accounts (examples fofaa4x3y145@melocc.cc and fofa6o4vg697@melocc.cc) plus passwords and JWTs. Rotating those free-tier tokens is described as producing tens of thousands of FOFA queries a day for exposed .env files, Docker configs, and Git repos. Hits are regex-parsed for OpenAI sk-proj keys and DeepSeek keys matching sk- followed by 32 hex characters. OpenAI keys are checked against api.openai.com and sorted into valid_no_balance (HTTP 429) or revoked (HTTP 401). DeepSeek balances are queried; the post names keys pulled from labibiyat.com and nyisu.com. The same control server, 134.175.71.194 (Tencent Cloud, Guangzhou), is described as hosting a GoTTY web terminal titled Pi – AI Coding Assistant (https://github.com/yudai/gotty), heartbeat bots that fake student reading time, and a scraper of 5,132 student records from the Fengxian campus of the Shanghai Publishing and Printing College, including campus-card balances and a QR payment-code module. VECERT says the operator is possibly in China and likely tied to Shanghai's academic community. Link keyhunter-llm-key-theft-2026-11, which also uses FOFA to hunt LLM keys.
attacks.initial_access: Mass FOFA account registration through a private catch-all mail domain, then searches for exposed .env files and git repos
ai_tooling_and_models: GoTTY web terminal (https://github.com/yudai/gotty), described as Pi – AI Coding Assistant
Stolen OpenAI and DeepSeek API keys
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Holders of exposed OpenAI and DeepSeek keys; VECERT also describes 5,132 student records at a Shanghai college campus
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. VECERT (VECERT-TI-2026-1107-B) says the operator is possibly in China and likely tied to Shanghai's academic community. No government or vendor attribution.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: At least 1,438 FOFA accounts. 5,132 student records described. Control server 134.175.71.194.
attacks.prevention_angle: Do not leave provider keys in .env files, Docker configs, or public git repos. Monitor api.openai.com for bursts of validation calls that return 429 or 401. Treat melocc.cc and the named control IP as suspicious. Rotate any key that appeared in a public env file.
attacks.source_notes: Control IP 134.175.71.194, melocc.cc, the 1,438-account count, example mailbox local-parts, labibiyat.com, nyisu.com, and the GoTTY panel name are from the VECERT Medium post. The mail-server IP is not listed. The same post gives 156.251.234.242 in the DNS section (mail, api, pop, imap, and smtp subdomains) and 156.233.234.242 in the infrastructure section (Cognetcloud, ASN 401701). Secondary write-ups disagree about which address is the Cognetcloud mail server, and the embedded screenshots were not independently re-resolved. Both addresses are omitted.

attacks.name: S-RM ARTEX in the wild - incident response host artifacts and TTPs

sources.title: S-RM: ARTEX in the Wild - Lessons from Responding to Agentic AI Attacks
ARTEX: Attackers apply agentic AI

attacks.ai_role_detail: Adversaries deploy ARTEX autonomous agents for full intrusion lifecycle automation, from initial compromise through identity/cloud/code/firewall pivots in under 24 hours, with documented MSP supply-chain pivots and persistent re-entry after containment
attacks.technique_summary: S-RM incident response analysis (Nov 6, 2026) documents real-world ARTEX deployment artifacts and TTPs from multiple IR engagements. Initial access via vulnerable web plugins and misconfigured upload endpoints; rapid credential harvesting and reuse; autonomous agents pivot through identity systems, cloud resources, code repositories, and firewall configurations within a single day. One case featured MSP supply-chain pivot; another deployed card skimmers on compromised e-commerce sites. Attackers demonstrated persistent re-entry capability after initial containment, shifting to Tor and VPS infrastructure after IP blocking. Forensic artifacts: /opt/artex/data/task/<task>/i<id>/ directory structure; compromised files and accounts tagged with i<id> markers; SQL injection signatures ARTEX' UNION SELECT 1-- and ARTEX'/**/AND/**/2>1--; HTTP User-Agent norma/0.4; ARTEX web console self-signed certificate (O=ARTEX, C=CN) displaying Autonomous pentest console branding; GitHub branches named artex-wtest-*; fake emails @example.invalid. Actor unnamed; attributed by S-RM incident response; confirmed AI involvement from recovered agent task logs and autonomous pivot patterns. Sophos X-Ops (Nov 10, 2026) separately reports activity at a small number of customers consistent with ARTEX or other AI-assisted tooling: webshell and SQL Server command execution, credential theft, lateral movement, rapid command bursts, and structured markers. Windows host markers are temporary files named i[variant]_. such as i12345_b2.ps1, paths beginning artx especially under C:\Windows\Temp, and command markers MARKER123 or ARTX123. Cloud markers are a service principal credential or role added by an application, and application sign-ins with a scripted user agent. Sophos file detections are Troj/Bckdr-SDA for a trojanized ARTEX Docker image (see badbyte-artex-backdoor-docker-2026-11), Troj/Loader-TU, Linux/Agent-KD, and ATK/Artex-A, ATK/Artex-B, and ATK/Artex-C. Published firewall and endpoint IPS signatures are 2313266, 2313265, 2313264, 2313263, 2313261, 2313259, 2313258, and 2313257. Sophos cites Microsoft's Storm-0940 attribution for the ConnectWise Cloud Backup case only; that name is not applied to the S-RM engagements.
attacks.initial_access: Vulnerable web plugins, misconfigured file upload endpoints
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Multiple organizations across sectors including e-commerce, MSPs; S-RM IR engagements 2026
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed actors; attributed by S-RM incident response teams; multiple distinct but tactically similar ARTEX deployments
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Multiple IR engagements 2026; identity/cloud/code/firewall compromise in under 24 hours; MSP supply-chain pivot in one case; card skimmer deployment in another; persistent re-entry after containment
attacks.prevention_angle: Patch vulnerable web plugins promptly; restrict and validate file uploads; implement strict authentication for admin interfaces; monitor for ARTEX forensic indicators (/opt/artex/ directories, i<id> file/account tagging, SQL markers, norma/0.4 UA, self-signed ARTEX certs); block Tor egress where not required; implement network segmentation to limit lateral movement; rotate credentials after suspected compromise; monitor for artex-wtest- GitHub branch patterns; scrutinize @example.invalid emails in logs; deploy EDR to detect autonomous pivot behaviors; implement MSP supply-chain security controls
attacks.source_notes: S-RM blog (Nov 6, 2026) primary source documenting IR artifacts from multiple ARTEX engagements; all forensic indicators (file paths, SQL markers, UA strings, certificate details, GitHub patterns) verified from S-RM analysis; unnamed adversaries due to ongoing investigations. Sophos X-Ops (Nov 10, 2026) adds Windows host markers and the listed IPS IDs. 2313260 and 2313262 are not in the published signature table, so they are omitted. Sophos describes the customer activity as consistent with ARTEX or other AI-assisted tooling, which is vendor-asserted and does not replace the S-RM task-log evidence. Storm-0940 is Microsoft's attribution for ConnectWise, cited by Sophos, and is not used as the actor for the S-RM cases.

attacks.ai_role_detail: Storm-3358 deploys ARTEX autonomous AI agents to automate intrusion lifecycle against Southeast Asian financial institutions, from initial reconnaissance through lateral movement and RAT deployment
attacks.technique_summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence (Nov 6, 2026) reports Storm-3358, Cambodia-based financially motivated actor, targeting Southeast Asian financial sector using ARTEX autonomous offensive agents. Censys fingerprinting (Silas Cutler) identifies exposed ARTEX control panels via console title starting ARTEX + Next.js signature, port 8787, open directories leaking attack kit configurations. Oct 2026 activity: ARTEX agents autonomously scanned targets, exploited anonymous file upload vulnerabilities and SSRF, used netcat/curl to pull WISP RAT, vshell, and AdaptixC2 C2 frameworks; deployed web shells; conducted brute-force and password-spraying attacks; performed lateral movement. C2 infrastructure: WISP C2 199.19.95.66-68, AdaptixC2 85.11.167.52. ARTEX control panel servers: 91.92.240.238, 85.11.168.45, 31.77.229.35, 178.16.54.129 (Microsoft post hunting query lists 178.15.54.129 - note IP discrepancy). Storm-3358 attributed by Microsoft; vendor-asserted AI involvement. Tools: AdaptixC2 (github.com/Adaptix-Framework/AdaptixC2), ARTEX fork (github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX; original Autumn-27/ARTEX repository down).

attacks.prevention_angle: Implement file upload restrictions and validation; patch SSRF vulnerabilities; monitor for ARTEX console fingerprints (title ARTEX + Next.js, port 8787); block known C2 IPs (199.19.95.66-68, 85.11.167.52, 91.92.240.238, 85.11.168.45, 31.77.229.35); detect anomalous autonomous scanning patterns; monitor netcat/curl downloading RATs; implement web application firewalls; enable brute-force protection; segment networks to limit lateral movement
attacks.source_notes: Microsoft Threat Intelligence blog (Nov 6, 2026) primary source; Censys Agentic Asbestos analysis (Silas Cutler) provides ARTEX fingerprinting methodology; all IOCs verified from sources; note IP discrepancy between main text (178.16.54.129) and hunting query (178.15.54.129) in Microsoft post. FBI FLASH-20261113-001, citing that Microsoft post, lists WISP C2 199.19.95.66-68, ARTEX servers 91.92.240.238, 85.11.168.45, 178.16.54.129, and 31.77.229.35, and C2 85.11.167.52 as active as of 6 November 2026. The FLASH table does not include 178.15.54.129. The same published addresses appear in the FLASH CSV. The FLASH asks defenders to hunt web shells, BLOODALCHEMY components, and the open-source RATs WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2. It describes BLOODALCHEMY as ARTEX-related C2 in the general TTP section. It does not say Microsoft found BLOODALCHEMY on these bank intrusions. A security-detections-mcp search for BLOODALCHEMY returned no Sigma, Splunk, or Elastic rule.

attacks.name: AIR Office Party, Anthropic document skills load an unchecked LD_PRELOAD library

sources.title: Office Party: Anthropic's Document Skills Load an Unchecked Shared Library
skills/docx/scripts/office/soffice.py

attacks.borderline_note: Air Security published a proof of concept. The article does not describe in-the-wild exploitation. Anthropic acknowledged the report and said the helper only runs inside a sandbox, which Anthropic treats as outside its security boundary.
attacks.ai_role_detail: The official Anthropic docx, pptx, and xlsx skills call scripts/office/soffice.py. If a Unix socket cannot be opened, that helper sets LD_PRELOAD to whatever file is already at the temp-directory path lo_socket_shim.so.
attacks.technique_summary: Air Security (Omri Saxena and Or Nevo; article dated Nov 5, 2026) found the issue in May 2026 and reported it to Anthropic. The docx, pptx, and xlsx skills, used by Claude document features and by the Claude Code document-skills marketplace, convert documents with python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf. The docx skill renders every written document to PDF through that helper. The same helper is used by the pptx and xlsx skills. If the helper cannot open a Unix socket, including under a sandbox, seccomp, or EMFILE, it sets LD_PRELOAD to a path under the process temp directory, lo_socket_shim.so, and execs LibreOffice. The helper does not check who owns that file or what is in it. Whoever writes it first is loaded into the LibreOffice process. Air's proof of concept planted the library directly in a Claude Code sandbox temp directory, and a second proof used a companion skill that unpacked the .so into /tmp while the agent wrote marketing copy. The load is Linux-only. macOS ignores LD_PRELOAD, so the library is not loaded there. Air writes that Anthropic acknowledged the report and considers the behavior outside its security boundary because the helper runs in a sandbox. As of the Nov 5 article, scripts/office/soffice.py on the repository main branch was unchanged since July 17 and still loaded the file at that path. A check of the same file on Nov 15, 2026 still showed _SHIM_SO built from tempfile.gettempdir() joined with lo_socket_shim.so, an early return when that file exists, and env["LD_PRELOAD"] set to it.
attacks.initial_access: A local writer places lo_socket_shim.so in the temp directory before the document skill runs soffice.py. Air demonstrated a direct plant and a companion skill. No remote exploitation is described.
ai_tooling_and_models: Anthropic skills repository, skills/docx, skills/pptx, and skills/xlsx (https://github.com/anthropics/skills)
Claude Code document-skills and Claude document features that call soffice.py
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Users of the official Anthropic document skills on Linux, including Claude Code sandboxes where the socket open fails. No victim organizations are named.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: No threat actor. Air Security reported the behavior in the official skill. Anthropic's response, as quoted by Air, is that the helper is outside Anthropic's security boundary.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: One helper shared by the docx, pptx, and xlsx skills. No exploitation count was published.
attacks.prevention_angle: Pin document skills and review scripts/office/soffice.py before enabling them. On Linux, alert when a process sets LD_PRELOAD to lo_socket_shim.so, and when a compiler writes that filename under /tmp before soffice.py runs. Do not treat an /etc/ld.so.preload file rule as coverage for this env-var path. macOS does not honor LD_PRELOAD for this load.
attacks.source_notes: The May 2026 discovery, the Nov 5, 2026 article date, Anthropic's sandbox response, and the July 17 unchanged claim are from Air Security. The Nov 15, 2026 file check is a read of https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/docx/scripts/office/soffice.py. The pptx and xlsx helpers were not re-read on that date; Air says they share this helper.
attacks.region_notes: No target geography. The behavior is in published skill code.

atlas_techniques.rationale: The load is in the official Anthropic document skills, not a third-party copy
The docx skill invokes soffice.py as part of rendering a document the agent just wrote

attacks.name: Apiiro finds Claude Code settings.local.json secrets in 1,122 public GitHub copies

sources.title: Coding Agents Are Leaking Your Secrets to GitHub
Someone Is Scanning for Your MCP Servers and AI Assistant Credentials

attacks.ai_role_detail: Choosing Yes, and don't ask again can save the exact approved shell command, secret included, in .claude/settings.local.json. Claude Code adds that path to the user's global git excludes, not to the repository .gitignore.
attacks.technique_summary: Apiiro (published Nov 5, 2026; updated Nov 8) searched public GitHub from Nov 1 to Nov 3, 2026, and found 104,185 copies of .claude/settings.local.json in 103,617 repositories. Of those, 1,122 files (1.1 percent) held at least one secret the researchers counted, 1,379 distinct secrets in that file alone: 636 provider-format keys and 743 passwords or tokens next to a public host. The count includes 379 database passwords, 122 Supabase service-role keys, 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 GitHub, GitLab, and npm tokens, 23 AWS keys, and 6 private keys. Adding history, the shared .claude/settings.json file, and saved agent transcripts brings the total to 2,539 distinct secrets in 1,994 repositories. The mechanism is Claude Code's own permission prompt. If the user picks Yes, and don't ask again, the allow rule stored in the project file can be the exact command, so a password after PGPASSWORD= or sshpass -p is written in plain text. Apiiro reproduced that with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1. The first time Claude Code creates the file inside a git repository it adds the path to the user's global git excludes. That rule stays on one computer, does not cover a folder that becomes a repository later, and is never written to the project's .gitignore. If the file is already tracked, later approvals are appended and the user is not told. In 539 of 1,105 repositories with a secret that Apiiro traced, a commit co-authored by Claude changed the file. On Nov 2, 2026 every secret-bearing copy Apiiro checked was still on the default branch. The median repository had first committed it 217 days earlier. Deleting the file left 734 further secrets in history across 509 repositories, and 211 forks of 74 repositories carried the same secrets. gitleaks flagged 564 of the 1,122 files and TruffleHog 643. Neither flagged 215. Apiiro names 63 organizations and says one confirmed a notified key had been live. No credential was tested. Boris Cherny, head of Claude Code, wrote on Hacker News on Nov 7 that the team was looking at auto mode and basic secret scanning, and that he believed exposed copies had been created manually. A separate SANS Internet Storm Center diary by Manuel Humberto Santander Peláez (July 13, 2026) records internet scans for /.claude/settings.local.json, /.claude/mcp.json, and /.cursor/mcp.json on an ordinary web host. That diary does not attribute the scans to this GitHub corpus.
attacks.initial_access: A developer approves an exact Claude Code shell command that contains a secret. The settings file is later committed, or was already tracked, so the secret is in a public repository and its history.
ai_tooling_and_models: Claude Code permission prompt, Yes and don't ask again
Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, used when Apiiro reproduced the save
other_tooling: git global excludes, which do not travel with the repository
attacks.victims_and_sectors: 63 organizations with a counted secret in a public allow list, plus individual developers. Apiiro's table includes a database vendor, a medical-records application, and other software companies. No organization is named.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: No named actor for the GitHub copies. The exposure is Claude Code writing secrets into a file that git then publishes. The July 2026 ISC diary documents separate scanning for the same paths.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: 104,185 public copies, 1,122 with a counted secret, 1,379 secrets in the current file, 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories once history, shared settings, and transcripts are included. 539 of 1,105 traced repositories had a Claude co-authored commit touching the file.
attacks.prevention_angle: Search the organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json, including git history, and rotate every secret those files ever held before deleting them. Add the local file to each repository .gitignore. Approve command patterns instead of one exact command, and reference secrets as variables such as $DB_URL so the saved rule does not hold the value. Scanners that only match known key formats miss passwords after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, and mysql -p.
attacks.source_notes: Counts, dates, the git-exclude behavior, the scanner gap, and Boris Cherny's Nov 7 comment are from the Apiiro post. Organization names are not in that post and are not added here. The July 13, 2026 path list is from the SANS ISC diary by Manuel Humberto Santander Peláez. The diary does not say those scans started the weekend of the Apiiro post.
attacks.region_notes: Apiiro does not name the countries of the 63 organizations. Public GitHub is not a victim region.

attacks.technique_summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence (Nov 5, 2026) reports unattributed cloud-credential harvesting campaign using ARTEX autonomous agent framework. Attackers conduct mass GitHub secret searches querying organization names, cloud keywords (Azure, AWS, Entra, Key Vault), and AI provider keys. ARTEX agents authenticate as compromised Azure Entra service principals, then autonomously enumerate and exfiltrate Azure Key Vault secrets, storage account keys, App Service configuration settings, AKS cluster credentials, SharePoint/OneDrive files, Microsoft Graph queries, Azure AI Studio keys, and Azure Foundry credentials within approximately 5 minutes per compromised tenant. Agents feature adaptive retry logic that automatically corrects Azure Resource Manager API version errors on failed calls, demonstrating autonomous error recovery. Campaign operates from IPs 199.19.77.84, Tor exit 199.19.77.18, 65.87.223.26, and 157.22.126.128. Microsoft notes median dwell time of 8 minutes from initial service principal authentication to complete key-vault enumeration, indicating highly automated credential-harvesting workflow targeting cloud and AI infrastructure. VulnCheck (Patrick Garrity, Nov 8, 2026) reports 199.19.77.84 hit VulnCheck canaries Nov 7 exploiting CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow /api/v1/validate/code endpoint). Agent staged Python using @exec decorator, _lf_probe() wrapper function, and |RAISE| exception-based exfiltration channel; dumped env/.env files and langflow.db; checked Docker socket and cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254; grepped for sk-, AIza, AKIA key patterns; read mem0 configuration; decrypted Langflow Fernet-encrypted variables. attacks.technique_summary: Nov 4, 2026: Acronis TRU discovered BOSSAI, a mesh of 12 AI agents (9 active, 3 inactive) operated by single actor 'bossjy' (aliases TIAN0517, lstjks) based in Hualien, Taiwan. Agents divided into infrastructure builders (Grok, OpenClaw, Claude Code) running commercial models, and offensive agents (Hermes, HalberdStrike, CyberStrike) running abliterated local models (DeepSeek-V4, Qwen 3.5 122B). Commercial models repeatedly refused attack commands, forcing use of locally-run abliterated models. Agent mesh targeted hundreds of organizations across government emergency services, banks, universities, military systems in 11 countries. Confirmed breaches at Taiwan emergency services (patient care records, 119 dispatch data), universities (Thailand SQL injection), and financial institutions. Operator ran mesh from home IP alongside legitimate businesses (gas store, K-beauty reseller, Facebook auto-post SaaS). Attack mesh generated high volumes of data with frequent hallucinations and false positives; agents sometimes refused lucrative targets (Honduran military base) due to autonomous scope decisions. MCP servers provided GitHub security, CVE lookup, OSINT, cloud auditing, Ghidra, Radare2, Playwright automation, and Kali Linux tools (nmap, sqlmap, Metasploit, Hydra). GPU fleet: RTX 4090s serving abliterated models via llama.cpp, plus 8 VPS nodes for proxying. OPSEC failures exposed entire operation: GitHub account linked to physical storefront, SSH sessions exposed home IP, credentials hardcoded throughout.

attacks.technique_summary: Financially motivated attacks against schools in Africa and Latin America used the open-source CyberStrikeAI implant. Initial access was through a compromised SQL Server. A C2-side LLM using MCP tools selected attack commands and achieved domain administrator privileges in three to four days. Techniques included a SystemUpdate scheduled task, certutil downloads, comsvcs.dll LSASS memory dumping, DCSync, and Golden Ticket generation.
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Schools in Africa and Latin America
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Kaspersky could not link the activity to a known group. Chinese-language script comments and UTC+8 control-server restarts suggest a Chinese-speaking operator.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Domain admin achieved in 3-4 days; multiple schools targeted
attacks.prevention_angle: Harden SQL Server; monitor for CyberStrikeAI indicators; detect SystemUpdate scheduled task creation; alert on certutil downloads; monitor comsvcs.dll LSASS dumps; detect DCSync activity; hunt for Golden Ticket use; block C2 infrastructure; review LOLBAS execution (certutil, comsvcs)

- Sigma: Suspicious LSASS Process Access (https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/process_creation/proc_creation_win_sysinternals_procdump_lsass.yml)

sources.title: SOCRadar STRU: KeyHunter Operation - Harvard Alumni Data, Stanford Applications and LLM Key Theft

attacks.ai_role_detail: leepsmarts harvests LLM API keys from misconfigured cloud infrastructure while using AI agents (Hermes, OpenClaw) to manage operations and conduct parallel academic fraud campaign
attacks.technique_summary: Nov 4, 2026: SOCRadar STRU discovered KeyHunter operation by leepsmarts (Chinese-speaking, UTC+8), active since Jan 2026. Two parallel tracks: (1) LLM API key theft: 2,233 API keys harvested (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek), 12 marked valid (0.54% yield), targeting 247 exposed LLM gateways on PaaS platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Railway, Render, Replit, Streamlit, Fly.io, Cloudflare Pages). Tools scan .env files, GitHub repos, and cloud metadata. (2) Academic fraud: 195 Harvard alumni records from Nov 2025 ShinyHunters torrent, application payment links for Stanford/UChicago/Wake Forest/Case Western/Central Michigan, accounts at NYU/UC Berkeley/Oregon State/UIUC/Colorado State. (3) Financial fraud: Harmony ONE crypto drainer, stolen Stripe merchant keys for card validation, CVVs from Chinese underground market. Infrastructure: 6 servers + Malaysia OpenClaw host, tied by PentAGI CA certificate. AI agents manage operations: Hermes Agent node runs AI_radar cron (every 240min) monitoring X/Twitter, HuggingFace, GitHub, arXiv for new LLM releases/quotas via grok-4.6 + Tavily proxy. Four-phase pipeline: Phase 0 (AI monitoring), Phase 1 (FOFA/Shodan reconnaissance), Phase 2 (env_hunter scans 50+ paths, fadidevv/keyhunter + bigzooooz/KeyHunter GitHub scrapers), Phase 3 (validation), Phase 4 (unified dashboard). OPSEC failure: directory listing on 209.112.91.74 exposed 110 files/37 directories including Telegram bot tokens, operational logs, stolen credentials. CVE-2026-41940 (CVSS 9.8, CISA KEV) exploit staged against UTN Argentina, Arizona Christian University, University of Utah. Real victim seed phrases captured by Harmony ONE drainer.

attacks.name: Load/Mine malicious Qwen2 models on Hugging Face
attacks.researcher: Shaked Chen, Eitan Chassid, Yotam Perkal

sources.title: Load/Mine: A malware campaign targeting Hugging Face and ModelScope

attacks.technique_summary: Malicious Qwen2 test models uploaded to Hugging Face (e.g. MENXIANGYU/qwen2-tiny) and mirrored on ModelScope. config.json auto_map field points to modeling_evil2.EvilModel which executes on trust_remote_code=True and vLLM versions before 0.14.0 without that flag (CVE-2026-22807). Payload runs fileless peakminer cryptominer via memfd_create, establishes .bashrc persistence, deploys reverse shells, and achieves GPUStack container escape. Models appear as legitimate Qwen2 variants for testing purposes.

attacks.scale_and_metrics: Multiple malicious models uploaded including MENXIANGYU/qwen2-tiny; exact victim count unknown
attacks.prevention_angle: Pin and verify model checksums; avoid trust_remote_code=True; update vLLM to 0.14.0 or later; monitor memfd_create usage; scan .bashrc for unauthorized changes; detect outbound cryptocurrency mining traffic; review model config.json auto_map fields; use model scanning tools
attacks.source_notes:
Relevant detection rules:
- Sigma: Suspicious Cron File Created (persistence via .bashrc) (https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/linux/file_event/file_event_lnx_susp_cron_file_created.yml)
- Sigma: Audio Capture via memfd_create (fileless execution pattern, can detect suspicious memfd_create usage) (https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/linux/auditd/lnx_auditd_audio_capture.yml)

attacks.name: Chainstack - ARTEX intrusion from a default-credential Grafana to production password hashes

sources.title: Incident report: what happened and what customers need to do
Chainstack reports production systems were reached in the late-October campaign
Chisel

attacks.ai_role_detail: Chainstack's Nov 10 update says the attacker used ARTEX. An unauthenticated internal MCP tool server, running as cluster-admin, was the command executor. That is a secondary case of an AI tool server being abused, not the initial entry.
attacks.technique_summary: Chainstack's incident page (created Nov 3, 2026, technical update Nov 10, page updated Nov 11) says an attacker reached production and customer account data, including password hashes. The Nov 10 update replaces the earlier unknown entry point. A test Grafana instance, deployed in July to a development Kubernetes cluster, was exposed to the internet with the default administrator credentials unchanged and without SSO or basic authentication in front. From Oct 26 at 19:26 UTC the attacker used Grafana's data-source proxy to reach internal services. A Grafana administrator can point a data source at any URL, and the proxy forwards the request. Over about two hours that reached dozens of internal services, including identity, database, automation, and monitoring. At 21:01 the proxy reached an internal MCP tool server that exposes Kubernetes operations to AI agents. It required no authentication, and its service account was bound to cluster-admin. Chainstack says network flows and the changes that followed show this server was the command executor; the individual tool calls were not recovered. The same night the attacker tested an internal workflow engine with names artx-check-* and artex-verify-*, created administrator users in the development identity provider, and replaced JavaScript in a development web app by mounting ConfigMaps over the served files. On Oct 27 the same loader was applied to staging and to the development Grafana. The loader referenced hxxps://silverbullet[.]icu/p/17fbad90-3094-4198-9b60-49fc852e331d/bootstrap.js and the marker window.__artx7f3a. No software vulnerability was exploited. Development machine credentials also worked in production. On Oct 29 those credentials and a BI-tool API key were used from 187.15.134[.]80. Between 17:03 and 17:12 a workflow was rewritten in the platform database so it ran shell commands, triggered with a valid webhook token through Grafana, then restored. That returned the automation pod's environment, its Kubernetes service-account token, and a machine identity. At 17:49 production Kubernetes secrets were listed from 18.237.52[.]142. On Oct 31, from 01:40 to 08:31, 187.15.134[.]45 bulk-read the production cloud secrets manager, created extra keys, and created a Kubernetes service account artx-sa with role artx-observer and token artx-sa-token. A short-lived pod on the host network took the node's cloud token from the instance metadata service. Another cluster ran a privileged pod with host networking and host PID and installed a static-pod relay to 185.242.233[.]68:39443. A compromised VPN peer key from that address reached the database network and flapped the tunnel, which is how the intrusion was noticed. Attacker pods queried production databases, including PostgreSQL pg_shadow on one instance. On Oct 30 a cron job ran Chisel (https://github.com/jpillora/chisel) as a reverse SOCKS tunnel to 185.242.233[.]68:10800, and a systemd timer named artx-guard beaconed to 185.242.233[.]68:8088/artx-beacon. The same host also served a VPN client on port 9331. Access paths were cut on Oct 31. Copied tokens kept working until 06:28 UTC on Nov 2. Chainstack assesses with high confidence that the attacker used ARTEX, from artx/artex markers such as artex-i37257-*, parallel paths, and chisel, and says the indicators do not match the actor-specific lists published for Vapor Panda, Storm-0940, or Storm-3358. Customer nodes, the console, and the API were not modified. Password hashes, organization and account names, member emails, and node credentials are treated as exposed. Payment card data is not stored. ATT&CK techniques Chainstack maps include T1078.001, T1078.004, T1609, T1610, T1611, T1053.003, T1053.006, T1552.005, T1552.007, and T1572.
attacks.initial_access: Internet-exposed test Grafana in a development Kubernetes cluster, left on the default administrator credentials, then Grafana's data-source proxy into an unauthenticated MCP tool server whose service account had cluster-admin
ai_tooling_and_models: Unauthenticated MCP tool server bound to cluster-admin, used as the command executor
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Chainstack, a blockchain infrastructure provider, and its customers' account records (organization names, account-holder names, member emails, password hashes) and node credentials, which Chainstack treats as exposed
attacks.region_notes: Chainstack lists offices in the United States and Singapore. The report does not say which country the compromised clusters ran in. Actor attribution is not a victim location.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Chainstack attributes the tooling to ARTEX with high confidence and says that does not identify the operator. None of the indicators match the actor-specific sets published for Vapor Panda, Storm-0940, or Storm-3358.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Development access from Oct 26 19:26 UTC. Production Kubernetes secrets read Oct 29 17:49 UTC. Production secrets-manager bulk reads Oct 31 01:40-08:31 UTC. Last use of a copied credential Nov 2 06:28 UTC. Customer-facing services kept running. Password hashes and node credentials are in scope. Card data was not stored.
attacks.prevention_angle: Do not publish a test Grafana, or any admin UI, without SSO or an equivalent extra login, and replace default administrator credentials at deploy time. Treat a data-source proxy as privileged: allowlist destinations and block cluster-internal addresses that are not approved data sources. An MCP or other AI tool server needs authentication and must not run as cluster-admin. Development credentials must not be valid in production. Alert on secret lists, bulk cloud secret reads, a new privileged or hostPath pod, a systemd timer, cron launching a tunnel, and the same VPN peer key presented from two addresses. artx and artex resource names are a hunt clue only when tied to this behavior.
attacks.source_notes: The Nov 10 technical section is the source for the Grafana entry, the MCP server, the ARTEX assessment, the IPs, and the hashes. The page was updated Nov 11. The Hacker News article is the Nov 3 report, before that section existed. Hashes are of application files the attacker modified to carry the loader, not of a second stage or of host binaries. Chainstack also published Grafana bundle hashes 07691e5949a123e313e1d589288e3831ec8ac30b90c45ab99d3b6ad07f23789a and 455473033f7ecbeafaa70e38f41f924377d54013efedeb0996ee84d3422c10ce, and test-page hashes 7c5925a3bc97983bfbfccdc514edb4dadbdb5b796a0747a764b0dcc4f103ea15 and b4a701949a1489e81754637238ed3f8177520f9f950e655f9357900d9e30aea8. Link barracuda-artex-cloud-key-intrusion-2026-11 and srm-artex-ir-host-artifacts-2026-11 for the i-counter artifact pattern.

atlas_techniques.rationale: The entry point was an internet-exposed Grafana. Chainstack says no software vulnerability was exploited; the data-source proxy and the unchanged default administrator account were abused.
An unauthenticated MCP tool server became the command executor, and Chainstack says the attacker used ARTEX.
Development credentials, a production secrets-manager bulk read, Kubernetes secrets, and the instance-metadata token were stolen.
The Grafana default administrator account, cloud service-account keys, and a VPN peer key were reused as valid accounts, including from development into production.

attacks.name: Cyera Research - Tampered copy of Anthropic's PDF skill carrying Linux Go backdoor system_linux

sources.title: Malicious Copy of Anthropic's PDF Skill Carries Linux Backdoor

attacks.ai_role_detail: Supply-chain attack impersonating Anthropic's official PDF skill; tampered skill archives contain 5.1 MB garble-obfuscated Linux Go backdoor exposing developer workstations to remote shell access
attacks.technique_summary: Cyera Research (Nov 3, 2026) discovered six skill archives impersonating Anthropic's official PDF skill, observed May 23 - July 14, 2026. Each archive contains 11 files byte-identical to upstream Anthropic pdf skill (github.com/anthropics/skills), but SKILL.md is truncated from 315 lines to 19 lines keeping official name and description while replacing Quick Start section with curl https://scan.100tal.com command, and adds 5.1 MB garble-obfuscated 64-bit Linux Go ELF binary system_linux. Binary features AES-256-GCM encrypted configuration with 0xAA XOR decryption revealing C2 81.70.101.115:2345 and attaches /bin/bash over raw TCP socket. Simplified Chinese strings in binary and UTC+8 archive timestamps indicate Chinese-language development environment. scan.100tal.com hostname linked to TAL Education Group infrastructure. Cyera notes attribution is unknown and could indicate targeted attack or internal security exercise. Cyera analyzed archives but did not observe live execution of system_linux backdoor. garble obfuscator (github.com/burrowers/garble) used to strip Go function names and identifiers. Demonstrates supply-chain risk where skill typosquatting or compromised distribution channels can deliver backdoors to AI developer environments.

attacks.ai_role_detail: Threat actors hijack enterprise LLM access, generate $100K-$1M USD fraudulent charges, monetize via LLM Mixers (illicit routing gateways), deploy agentic workloads with Manus framework
attacks.technique_summary: Multiple threat clusters (UNC6993, Jet Night operators, D1337-KAIROS) hijack enterprise access to LLMs across AWS Bedrock, Azure, GCP. Initial access via exposed cloud identity tokens (IAM, Service Account keys, GitHub PATs, session tokens), stolen LLM API keys from public GitHub, exploited web app vulnerabilities, LiteLLM CVE-2026-40217 (/key/regenerate endpoint rebind). UNC6993 used session hijacking page masquerading as app portal to steal JSON payloads with active access tokens. Threat actors enable LLM services, create API keys, provision GPUs, subscribe Pay-As-You-Go, deploy LiteLLM/new-api/gcli2api gateways, host Manus agent framework with SearXNG metasearch. Monetize via LLM Mixers (Jet Night at jet-night.com $60/month unlimited, ai-relay on lookalike domains, newapi.pro). Stealthy credential validation sweeps with max_tokens=1. Fraudulent charges $100K in single day, cumulative $1M per org. Division of labor between initial access and downstream monetization. Fireworks AI (Nov 9, 2026) reports Oct 23 third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks R&D breached; Oct 24 attacker entered via provider, ran unauthorized workload; reached account/billing data and, for some customers, secrets, datasets, partly trained model weights. Fireworks attributes to financially motivated LLMjacking group selling access to illicit routing gateways; GTIG/Mandiant report referenced; Unit 42 forensics. Notion, a Fireworks customer, published a downstream notice: Fireworks told Notion on Nov 2 that a small dataset of Notion AI synthetic test data was accessed; Notion disconnected and deleted Fireworks data by the morning of Nov 3; on Nov 6 Fireworks said customer data may have been accessed; on Nov 8 Fireworks confirmed the final dataset; on Nov 9 Notion contacted affected customers. The exposed data is Notion AI Insights chat transcripts for under 1 percent of workspaces, mostly unattributable (no user or workspace labels, and no tool-call results). No other Notion features were affected. Notion told affected customers to treat the transcripts as exposed and to rotate secrets pasted into Notion AI. On Nov 11 Notion revoked exposed Notion API keys found in affected user messages.

attacks.technique_summary: Multiple malicious MCP servers published on npm. @ifasn/md-doc-mcp and @ifasn/mmdd-doc-mcp probe cloud metadata endpoints, read sensitive files (/etc/shadow, SSH keys, .env, Kubernetes tokens), and exfiltrate to 121.199.24.94. @ifasn/ms-doc-mcp versions 2.0.9 and 2.1.1 (GHSA-556m-xfwj-7wff, MAL-2026-18603) use imdsAudit() function to steal Alibaba Cloud IMDS credentials from 100.100.100.200 and exfiltrate them over MCP stdout. gadgethumans-mcp versions 1.0.10-1.0.15 leak WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY environment variable in HTTP header on every tool call. Published with OpenSSF GHSA-rvw8-22w3-342v, GHSA-4h5p-w547-9qmv (Nov 2) and Leitwacht LWA-2026-13557, LWA-2026-13564. Aug 12, 2026: Pillar Security disclosed Deadbugz malicious MCP server (GitHub zellkernel) stealing AI model credentials and API keys. Feb 20, 2026: Socket discovered SANDWORM_MODE campaign spreading malicious MCP servers targeting developer credentials. November 9-12 additions: @rfewqa-fes/mnm-doc-mcp 1.0.0 (MAL-2026-19148, Amazon Inspector) ships an inert MCP stub in index.js. Its package.json pulls the only dependency, node-health-utils, as an off-registry tarball over plain HTTP from http://121.199.24.94/dl/health-utils-1.0.0.tgz, so whatever that host serves, including lifecycle scripts, runs at npm install. package.json sha256 f8ad55746cfac30b0a9401634b2728afc93e6dc20a85c511efd0ed312e466e8d. Package tarball sha1 f3ad664b487c4041e7e66e5744656ed44e1a6f6a. GitHub also marked @lemili9804/mcp-weather-server 1.0.3 and 1.0.6 (GHSA-qwfq-cw9x-55x4), mcp-contract-tester all versions (GHSA-34p7-qcxm-gc39, MAL-2026-19082), and @bestcoolman/dev-mcp (GHSA-vgx2-8w7x-xr8v, MAL-2026-19052) as malware, with no published behavior write-up. The entry now covers PyPI as well. my-mcp-server-driving-license-ocr 0.1.3 (MAL-2026-19204, GHSA-wg5f-m5mv-gmjg, Amazon Inspector, Nov 12) exposes an MCP tool, analyze_image, described as driving-license OCR. It POSTs the caller's image URLs or base64 bytes over plain HTTP to the hardcoded http://42.193.222.35:8000/ocr_pic and overwrites any MY_API_URL setting so the destination cannot be changed. karma365-mcp 2.1.0 (GHSA-72xc-q3v8-7grp, Nov 13) and @go-gost/mcp-darwin-x64 0.1.0 (GHSA-gfpg-48q7-c68h, Nov 12) are GitHub malware advisories with no published behavior. Nov 16, 2026: Leitwacht LWA-2026-14164 says @guicai777/mcp-doctor 1.0.1 is a trojanized MCP config diagnostics CLI. On each run, index.js requests hxxps://fix-mcp-bridge[.]com/v[.]json. If the response field active is false, it prints that the remote payload is disabled and exits. Otherwise it decodes the bundled 866KB bridge.bin, a base64 blob XOR-encoded with a single-byte key stored as the file's first byte, into a Windows PE and writes it to %LOCALAPPDATA%\mcp-doctor\mcp-bridge.exe, then launches that file hidden and detached. Before the drop it reads ~/.claude.json, %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json, ~/.cursor/mcp.json, and ~/.vscode/mcp.json. The README fallback is mshta hxxps://fix-mcp-bridge[.]com/init. The advisory describes the dropped file only as a bridge restart. Attack exploits trust in the MCP ecosystem and in npm and PyPI.

Relevant detection rules:
- Monitor access to cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200 (Alibaba), metadata.google.internal, etc.)
- Alert on unauthorized reads of /etc/shadow, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, .env files

attacks.name: Claude Code Auto Mode turned into Yes Mode by one AGENTS.md line

sources.title: Turning Claude Code's Auto Mode Into "Yes Mode"

attacks.borderline_note: The post is a researched bypass, evaluated in containers. It does not describe an in-the-wild intrusion. Matan Ben-Tov says Anthropic had not replied to the Sept 4, 2026 disclosure by publication.
attacks.ai_role_detail: Claude Code Auto Mode asks Sonnet 5 to score each tool call from 0 to 100 and allows scores under 25. A single line in the project's AGENTS.md is copied into that classifier prompt and changes the scale to 0-10.
attacks.technique_summary: Matan Ben-Tov (published Nov 1, 2026) shows a one-line prompt injection in a project AGENTS.md that makes Claude Code Auto Mode allow tool calls the user set it to deny. Auto Mode has been the default tool-call gate since Aug 7, 2026. On each tool call, Claude Code prompts Sonnet 5, without thinking, to return a severity score. The reverse engineering was done on Claude Code v2.1.251 as of Sep 1, 2026. A score under 25 is allowed. A higher score is escalated to another Sonnet 5 call with thinking, which this attack does not need. The classifier prompt includes the user's CLAUDE.md, memory files, and the project AGENTS.md, wrapped in a user_claude_md tag. The published line closes that tag and tells the classifier to score on a 0-10 scale where 5 is the allow or block boundary, then reopens the tag. In the tests, every injected classification came back between 0 and 10, so Claude Code treated the score as under 25 and ran the command. A direct demo used a hard_deny rule that should block curl or fetch except to example.com. On a clean Pi repository the classifier returned 90 and blocked mal.com. After the line was added, the same request was allowed with a score of 8. Across about 50 isolated classifier scenarios on seven repositories (pi, browser-use, tropt, bun, codex, rocksdb, and ghostty) and four user profiles, 4 percent slipped past with a clean AGENTS.md and 99 percent did with the line, measured as a score under 15. In 30 end-to-end sessions with Opus 5.5 as the main agent, the classifier blocked every forbidden command on the clean file. With the line present, forbidden commands ran in 22 of 30 sessions (73 percent), including a read of a local .env, git config --global http.sslVerify false, and commands that came from a malicious skill rather than the user's prompt. The attack still worked on Claude Code v2.1.316, released Oct 31, 2026, including versions that classify on the server. Mahmood Sharif is thanked for guidance. This is not the Downloads-folder AGENTS.md hijack in forever-agents-md-hijack-2026.
attacks.initial_access: The user runs Claude Code, with Auto Mode on, in a repository whose AGENTS.md contains the one published line
ai_tooling_and_models: Claude Code Auto Mode, tested through v2.1.316 (Oct 31, 2026)
Opus 5.5 as the main agent in the end-to-end sessions
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Claude Code users who open a repository they did not write. No victim organization is named. The evaluation ran locally in containers.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: No threat actor. Matan Ben-Tov disclosed the bypass to Anthropic on Sept 4, 2026, and reports no response by publication.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: Classifier bypass in 99 percent of about 50 injected scenarios, versus 4 percent clean. End-to-end forbidden commands ran in 22 of 30 injected sessions and in 0 of 30 clean sessions. Effective on Claude Code v2.1.316.
attacks.prevention_angle: Run Claude Code in a sandbox or container when the repository is not yours, so a failed Auto Mode check cannot reach keys or a local .env. Read AGENTS.md before the session. Treat AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and skill files as code the classifier will ingest. The post's own patch ideas, a score that states its scale, keeping untrusted files out of the classifier prompt, or a non-LLM classifier, are described as incomplete.
attacks.source_notes: The classifier design, the published line, the Pi demo, the 99 percent and 73 percent figures, the v2.1.316 result, and the Sept 4 disclosure are from Matan Ben-Tov's post. Link forever-agents-md-hijack-2026, which uses a different AGENTS.md lure.
attacks.region_notes: No target country. The evaluation repositories are public codebases used as fixtures.

attacks.ai_role_detail: The tampered package was a copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension placed on the cache Cursor used for its VS Code marketplace. Anthropic did not publish that copy.
attacks.technique_summary: Cursor's Nov 13, 2026 update says the attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks. Fireworks exposed that key. The attacker copied a read-only bucket used to share data with Fireworks. The bucket held limited coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode and were permitted for training. A small number of traces had unredacted credentials. Less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed. From those credentials the attacker reached select SaaS tools, then select archived non-production Cursor repositories, limited customer-support data and email, product usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some coding-agent conversations, and credentials users had sent to support. On Oct 29, using a stolen credential, the attacker placed malicious unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace. Anthropic did not publish this copy. It was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product. Open VSX never had the malware. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions that day potentially received it. The copies were available for about 11 hours. The marketplace was taken offline, and a hosting provider took down the attacker's server. The last attacker activity Cursor saw was Nov 1, and it was blocked. Traces were exposed for fewer than 0.05% of non-Privacy-Mode users, who were notified. Privacy Mode prompts and code were not affected. Microsoft's Oct 30 analysis of the copies that were served, anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, describes a loader in extension.js that collected hostname, username, and environment variables matching secret patterns, added SSH key svc-telemetry to authorized_keys, opened a reverse SSH tunnel to tunnel@134.209.82.225, and beaconed to :8099/beacon. Persistence was a com.apple.sysmond LaunchAgent on macOS, an @reboot cron job on Linux, and a SysMon scheduled task on Windows. The marketplace window Microsoft and Cursor's earlier notice described was Oct 29, about 5:27 AM to 4:35 PM ET.
attacks.initial_access: Stolen access key that Cursor had issued to Fireworks, then a stolen credential used to place unauthorized Claude Code extension copies on the Cursor marketplace cache. Open VSX did not carry the malware.
attacks.victims_and_sectors: Cursor users who requested the specific cached extension versions on Oct 29, and customers whose non-Privacy-Mode traces or support credentials were in the copied bucket. Production systems and customer code repositories were not described as affected.
attacks.attribution_or_cluster: Unnamed. Cursor published the Fireworks-key root cause on Nov 13, 2026. No country is stated.
attacks.scale_and_metrics: At most 5,000 users potentially received the cached copies, which were available for about 11 hours. API credentials were exposed for less than 0.01% of customers. Traces were exposed for fewer than 0.05% of non-Privacy-Mode users. Tampered versions were anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313.
attacks.prevention_angle: Rotate credentials that were in coding-agent traces or sent to support if Cursor notified the account. Review SSH authorized_keys for svc-telemetry, outbound SSH to 134.209.82.225, LaunchAgent com.apple.sysmond, @reboot cron, and a SysMon scheduled task. Do not treat Open VSX as the source of this copy.
attacks.source_notes: The Fireworks access key, the read-only bucket, the 0.01% and 0.05% figures, the marketplace cache, the 5,000-user bound, the 11-hour window, and the Nov 1 last-seen activity are from Cursor's Nov 13, 2026 update. The loader, SSH key svc-telemetry, tunnel 134.209.82.225, beacon on port 8099, and the macOS, Linux, and Windows persistence names are from Microsoft's Oct 30 analysis. The earlier GitHub-repository explanation is not the root cause Cursor published on Nov 13.

attacks.ai_role_detail: Adversary creates 800+ fake GitHub repos mimicking legitimate AI skills, MCP servers, and Cursor rules; optimizes for LLM recommendation via SEO and naming; agents recommend malicious packages to users
attacks.technique_summary: Oct 30, 2026: Island Security identified 'FakeGit' campaign: 800+ fake GitHub repositories impersonating popular AI skills, MCP servers, Cursor rules, and Claude Code extensions. Repos use typosquat/combosquat names (e.g., cursor-rules-best-practices, mcp-server-github-enhanced, claude-code-skills-security), contain trojanized npm/PyPI packages or malicious install scripts. Adversary optimized repo metadata (README, topics, stars, forks) to rank highly in LLM tool recommendations: when users ask agents find me a GitHub MCP server or what Cursor skills should I use?, agents recommend FakeGit repos from search results. Payloads: Shai-Hulud variants, Discord webhook exfiltration, npm/PyPI worms, SSH backdoors. Island tracked 2,400+ installations from agent recommendations Oct-Nov 2026. Island reports the repositories deliver SmartLoader, which establishes persistence and installs StealC to steal credentials, active sessions, and other sensitive data. Attack exploits agent trust in GitHub search ranking and lack of package verification.
attacks.initial_access: AI agent recommends malicious GitHub repo in response to user query; user clones/installs per agent suggestion
attacks.victims_and_sectors: 2,400+ installations tracked Oct-Nov 2026 from agent recommendations; AI developers using agent-assisted package discovery

attacks.prevention_angle: Verify GitHub repos before install (check org, stars, age, commit history); use allowlisted skill/MCP sources; implement agent guardrails to warn on unverified packages; educate users not to blindly trust agent recommendations; review install scripts; use SCA tools; prefer official sources (Anthropic MCP registry, Cursor skills directory); flag typosquat patterns
attacks.source_notes: Island Security analysis is the live source for the FakeGit SmartLoader and StealC chain. The previously cited SecurityBreak post returned HTTP 404 and was removed. First documented campaign explicitly optimizing malware for LLM recommendation engines (agentbaiting). Represents new supply chain threat vector where adversaries target agent search/recommendation behavior rather than direct user search. Detection: monitor agent-initiated GitHub clones, alert on typosquat repo names (edit distance to popular repos), check for new GitHub accounts with multiple similar repos, review repos with inflated stars/forks but low commit activity, flag repos created after popular tools rise, scan for SmartLoader/StealC signatures.

sources.title: Activity using ARTEX agentic AI

attacks.technique_summary: ARTEX planner agent activity observed Sep 24-Oct 27 2026 by Unit 42. Agent autonomously harvested source maps, OpenAPI specifications, and runtime-config.json files. Attempted OAuth redirect URI abuse and password spraying. Successfully self-registered on exposed APIs without authentication. Read approximately 50 MB of data. Wrote data to an unauthenticated development document store. Microsoft tracks related activity as Storm-0940 with Oct 21 observations. Unit 42's Nov 11, 2026 post (Cuong Dinh, Richard Emerson, Samantha Stallings), ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools, adds incident-response and Managed Threat Hunting cases where ARTEX turned password-reset pages and exposed APIs into cloud access in under a day. Behavioral hallmarks in that post: bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25 to 31 seconds; a pivot within a minute of a credential download; more than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes; a GET to the same path after almost every successful write; canary values evil.com, test@example.com, and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12; and polling every 48 seconds. As of October 2026 Unit 42 counted 609 internet-facing ARTEX hosts and 1,323 CyberStrikeAI hosts, with 21 running both. The framework is https://github.com/RuoJi6/ARTEX.

attacks.prevention_angle: Authenticate all API endpoints including development; remove source maps from production; restrict OpenAPI spec access; validate OAuth redirect URIs; implement API registration controls; monitor for automated reconnaissance patterns; detect bulk configuration file access; alert on unauthenticated document store writes; review Storm-0940 indicators
attacks.source_notes:
Microsoft tracks related activity as Storm-0940 with Oct 21 observations

Relevant detection rules:
- Monitor for bulk access to source map files (.map.js, .js.map)
- Alert on OpenAPI specification downloads (openapi.json, swagger.json, api-docs)
- Detect runtime-config.json and similar configuration file access patterns
- Monitor for OAuth redirect URI manipulation attempts
- Alert on password spraying patterns (multiple authentication attempts across accounts)
- Detect unauthenticated API registration/account creation
- Monitor writes to development document stores from unexpected sources
- Track volume of API data reads (spike detection for ~50 MB threshold)
- Note: API reconnaissance detection typically requires application-level logging, WAF rules, and API gateway monitoring. No direct Sigma rules exist for OpenAPI/source map harvesting; requires custom rules based on web server access logs and application audit trails.
